THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 139 P9l TiE DRINK QUESTION. ment and a walk to a neighbouring " pub would settle the coming vote. And yet lam A BIT OF BIOGRAPHY. NOT A TERTOTALLIM. What inconsistency! I have never felt on this question that example did much good, nor have I much faith in the various prohibitive reforms put to the front in Englani My views under the first heading are well put in the " Literary World" of March 27, P, 286 under the heading of "indepen- dent Pleasures and Public-Houses." For a few years during my youth, I lived just on the borders of that highly aristocratic district in Manchester known as Angel Meadow. Many a time since then have I wandered through it, and taken quiet notes of the havoc drink Was working. Yes, drink; but drink was only a secondary cause. Fancy a man with a family and only earning from 15$. to 20z1. ver week preserving a steady persistent determination to keep respectable. Of course I am dealing with men such as are found in the ordinary common la- bouring class. Again, a phlegmatic man is but little sensitive to stimulus. When its influence wears off, there is little reaction, but let another man, of fine nervous organization, take a glass of spirits, and every nerve in his body tingles and leaps. Is not the present day civilization making us all more nervous I The body becomes run down, and says Dr. Beard," When the nervous system loses, through any cause, much of its nervous force, so that it cannot stand upright with ease and comfort, it leans on the nearest and most convenient artificial support that is capable of temporarily propping up the enfeebled frame." Now what I insist upon is, that until we take Dr. Richardson's advice and cease to keep men at work "until they are fagged out" we must expect the nervous portion to become drunkards, and the phlegmatics, such as myself, to be able to do with or without it, this latter depend- ing upon firmness of character as to being abstainers or otherwise. 810, Bay-st., San Francisco.
BY IL WHITHAM.

It may be allowable for me to say a few words on this question. In doing so, I propose to draw a little upon my own experience. When I was about fourteen years of age, my father found himself in Sheffield, having lost a considekable sum of money through the treachery of a partner in business. Not quite penniless, he still had not enough to enable him him to keep a growing family around him in idleness. The advertisements in Sheffield papers were looked up, resulting in my being placed in a whitesmith's shop. Here I stayed near upon three years. ten pounds being paid as a premium on my indentures being made out, and ten pounds having ultimately to be paid to break them. My master was a clever workman,but a fearful drunkard. Not only this, but the head workman, under whom I was placed, was also an inveterate drunkard. I have often thought the experience of years I passed during the period of my residence in Sheffield's smoky town ought to have made me evtr after one of the staunchest of prohibitionists. It did not; I look upon people who join the ordinary temperance societies, as rather failing in what seems to be their life's work. Their very isolation cuts them off from the great bulk of the people. Their work has to be done in a missionary fashion; the people don't care for missionaries. And I have fora number of years been quite certain that the habits of temperance, early planted within me, were sure, and good for me, and would react beneficially to those with whom I come in active contact every day. More especially has this been so during the past fifteen years. However, this is only my opinion; it need not disturb either our abstaining editor, or any of my good readers. The first thing I remember in my new quarters was that the new apprentices (I may say there were two of us bound at the same time), must be initiated into the mysteries of what is called in this city by the phrase "RUSHING THE GROWLER," or in otter words going with the can for beer. Yes, we were no sooner installed in our positions in the ' shop than master and man "went on a drunk." The boss generally kept it up for about three weeks,and ' would divide his time pretty equally between the shop and the " pubs " in the neighbourhood. All the publicans would either chalk up for him, or lend him as much money as he wanted when he was drinking or drunk. No doubt they were always honest with him, and never put down a sovereign when it was only half a sovereign. Every time he came into the shop the bellows would stop, and the anvil ceased ringing, and" now Harry," or "now Jack, fetch some beer," would be shouted out. All would gather around and I would pour the beer out. Jack and I were expected to take our share. But in this we were very stupid. We had both left good homes and were neither used to beer drinking nor yet used to such low depths. Poor Jack didn't stand it long.

SLEDGE HAMMER AND STADVATION soon sent him home to die. The house was close to the shop and when the anvil was quiet for any length of time,the "missis"would look in; we used to ring the anvil a bit to deceive her, but when this was not done in she would walk. The presence of that woman is with me to-day as strong as it was thirty-three years ago. She was a fine big woman, a devout Roman Catholic, and had more Of the mas- culine than the feminine about her. She would first give all the men a rating. Then we two lads for fetching beer would have a lecture, finishing up with marching the boss into the house, when, after he had slept off the beer, he would protest and vow all manners of good things, ending generally with walking out with her into the town. • These excur- sions of theirs, during a recess in the fuddling pro- gramme, were always a source of fun for the neighbours. He would get some money while she was with him, buy her some article of dress and send her home while he went to look after business. If he came home that night, it would be as drunk as a lord, but he seldom came into the house of his own accord while the "drunks" lasted. I remember one night, Jack and I having been to spend the evening with my own folk, we returned somewhat earlier than we intended. The house was all in darkness, and I had occasion to go into the upper yard. While there I heard a dismal snor- ing noise, which rather disturbed me. Jack in the meantime had gone for the key. Coming down into the lower yard I saw "Old Amory," I the boss hanging in the corner. He had used his necktie for this purpose. I ru.shed into the corner, lifted his body across my shoulder; I was a big strong lad at that time, and there waited for Jack. When he came we cut the tie and carried him into the house. After fetching the " missis "and doctor, we had to set to bringing him back again to life, for he was all but gone. A few weeks after this be was cut down again in the closet. This sort of thing went on for two years and a half. Allow me to write here, that I should not have told this weari- some tale had either of my parents been now living. They in the meantime had removed to Warrington, and I know my dear mother seldom laid her head on the pillow without wondering about, and pray- ing for, her "poor lad in Sheffield." The end of this came however. I have seen the man with whom I worked sell the bread out of the house for beer, when even his wife, and children were repeatedly corning to the shop with starved and hungry looks. begging him for money. She was a good woman and often made me a quiet seat by her fireside. I have seen her face one mass of cuts and bruises; she had fits and whenever he struck her would go right into one, falling against anything, and him too sodden to help her. He would be teetotal at times, and would mount the platform. During one of his fits, I joined the Society, and I remember for several Sundays I delivered temperance tracts around Sheffield. Well, near the close of the third year of my living in this house, where I had often to steal the food, or else starve, a change tame so far as I was concerned. The master had drunk himself into a fearful state. Sleeping one night across the hearth in a cutler's shop, a cinder had rolled to his elbow and burnt through his coat. It would have been nothing, had the man been healthy. This burn in a short time mortified and a dread ftsl state of

ment being deferred as can be urged in the case of a local authority borrowing money for the execution of works which will not be completed and become remunerative for many years, for if the Company pay the interest covenanted to be paid by them the Cor- poration will be receiving probably over £1 10s. or £1 per cent. per annum, as the case may be, in excess of the interest payable on the moneys raised by them under the bill. As the clause is at present drawn no period is prescribed within which the sinking fund shall be sufficient to redeem the debt incurred by the Corporation under the bill. The Board are strongly of opinion that such a period should be prescribed, and that the present clause should be recast in accordance with the principles which regulate the clauses ordinarily inserted in local Acts under which borrow- ing powers are conferred on local authorities. The Board submit that the proposal at present contained in the clause, which is that the Corporation shall yearly pay to the credit of the sinking fund 'an amount equal to one pound for every hundred pounds of the balance of the Canal Loan Account for the time being,' is one which cannot properly be acceded to, inasmuch as it is impossible to tell beforehand what its effects would be as regards the prolongation of the period within which the debt incurred by the Corporatien under the bill would be repaid, and whether the result might not be to allow the Corporation a longer period for the redemption of the debt than is allowed by the Standing Orders (see Stand- ling Order No. 173 a, House of Commons.) The Board do not clearly understand what are the object and effect of the proviso to the present clause. It seems clear, how- ever, that it is intended to diminish the amounts of the payments which would have otherwise to be made into the sinking fudd under the earlier part of the clause. And it is by no means clear that its effect would not be 1 to exempt the Corporation from any obligation to sot aside a sinking fund, if the Corporation were annually Ito receive from the Company a hundredth part of the lbalance for the time being owing by them to the Corpor- ation. If this is the effect of the clause, no sinking fund need in such a case ever be established, and the debt incurred under the bill by the Company need never be wholly repaid by them to the Corporation. If the I object of the proviso is to enable the Corporation to take I credit, when calculating the annual payments to the sinking fund, for any payments made to the fund in excess of the required annual payments, the Board suggest that this power, if required, should be given in accordance with precedents which have been adopted by Parliament in recent sessions."

THE BILL IN COMMITTEE. The Manchester Ship Canal Loan Bill, by which it is proposed that the Corporation should on the security of the rates of the city raise and lend £3,000;000 for the completion of the canal, was considered on Thursday by a Committee of the House of Commons. Mr. Pember, Q.C.• for the promoters, explained that in consequence of the death of the contractor, the purchase of the plant, and the acquisition of additional land, it was absolutely necessary to obtain this f u rther a mount. If the money were not forthcoming the works would be checked indefinitely, and the non-completion of the canal would be a disaster not only to Manchester but to Lancashire and other counties. He urged that there was comparatively little risk incurred by the proposed loan, which would yield 4-1, per cent., and that if even the canal proved a foilure • the addition to the rates would not exceed one shilling 'in the pound. Sir Joseph Lee gave evidence as to the difficulty of raising the money,and also as to the market price of the shares, after which the Mayor (Mr. Alderstan Mark) was examined, and, said it was the desire of the Corporation to see the enterprise succeed,. for they believed the canal would greatly benefit trade. He was satisbed that £3,000,000 would complete the undertaking, and said the ratepayers approved of the proposal:. Mr. Pope, Q.C. for the railway companieer opposed the billrholding that it was manifestly unfair that theyshould be rated practically to create competi..- tion with their own lines. The Committee decided that the preamble of the bill was proved, and expressed their intention of going through the clauses to-day. It was Intimated by Mr. Pope that the railway companies would carry their opposition to the other House.

It is estimated that the costs in the Baccarat case, which in due course of law will fall on the, plaintiff, amount to not le t:1 tnAn £5,000,

The Prince (): Wales, on leaving the court on Min4ay aternoon, presented the superintendent of the cearts of Justice, Mr. G. M. Ilantler, with a handsome gold pencil case, in recognition of the attention and care bestowed upon him during his attendance at the trial of the baccarat case.

To a dozen different people has been assigned the infamy of having betrayed the secret of the doings at, Tranby Croft, and all sorts of motives have been attributed to the vengeance-seeking Judas. I believe it will be found i that the story was blurted out, without an arriere pensee, by one of the valetaille, who had heard it talked about, and whose presence at a discussion was as highly estimated as was that of her cha sseur by the Empress Catherine at her toilette.

A good deal of nonsense has been talked about the swearing of the Prince of Wales in the baccarat case. It has been put about that was sworn at his own request, but that it is not usual to ad- minister the oath to a personage in his exalted posi- tion, his word being deemed sufficient. This is all wrong H.ILII. went into court, and gave his evi- &rice as a subject of her Majesty. He was subject, not Prince, while he was under the jurisdiction of the court. He rose with the rest on the judge's entry as a mark of respect to the Sovereign's repre- sentative, and he was sworn in the same way as an ordinary witness without any qUestion arising.

Some amusement, has been caused by the evident earnestness with which Sir William Gordon Cum- ming is represented to have resented the fact that credence was given to charges made by "inexperi- enced boys," namely, Mr. Lycett Green, Mr. A. S. Wilson, and Mr. Berkeley Levett. This is a conamon way with Army men and old clubmen. They get into it at school, where fifth and sixth form boys talk of boys in the lower school as youngsters. Later on in life, in the messroom and club smoke- room,the men over forty treat every fellow under thirtff-five as "a mere boy, my dear sir." The ex- pression is only intended to mean that the " boy's " experience is not ripe.

Interest is centred in the future position of Sir William Gordon-CumminY. There are persons bold enough to suggest that he will continue to be re- ceived in society as if nothing had happened, but that is impossible. The sympathies of society are with him,but it is impossible to overrule the verdict of a jury. It will have to be acted on at the Horse Guards, and at the clubs of which Sir William has long been a member. He will have to go with sad- ness, but none the less without standing on the order of his going.

A précis of the proceedings of the baccarat ease wa telegraphed to Balmoral every evening, last w,.elc for the information of the Queen, who has ex- pressed her displeasure respecting the course of events at Tanby Croft in such very strong terms that it would not surprise me if these unfortunate incidents were to cause Lord Coventry's resignation et his office in the household. The Queen is angry with everybody who has figured in the case, and I would not give much for Mrs. Arthur Wilson's chance of an invitation to any Buckingham Palace or other Court function, although Mr. "Jack" has just been elected a member of the Marlborough Club, which is "run "under august patronage.

No conference has yet been held on the Front Opposition Bench as to the course to be taken on the second reading of the Education Bill. It is, however, practically resolved that nothing shall be done to endanger the passage of the Bill, though the number of amendments already placed on tLe paper by private members point to prolonged dis- cussion.

Mr. Victor Cavendish took his seat in the House of Commons on Monday, being introduced by Lord Ilartington and Mr. Barnes. He was loudly cheered on both sides of the House. In appearance he greatly resembles Lord Hartington. The hon, gentleman took his seat on the back benches, shak- ing hands cordially with Mr. T. W. Russell, Mr. Lea, and Mr. Bolitho.

The papers announced a few days ago that Lady Florence Cecil had been confined of A son. This is an important and interesting event, for Lady Florence (th, eldest daughter of Lord Lathom) is the wife of Lord William Cecil, Rector of Hatfield, the second son of Lord Salisbury, and as his elder brother, Lord Cranborne, has no children, this infant is the ultimate heir to the Marquisate and the family estates.

The announcement that the German Emperor is to visit the manufacturing districts and "some of the great towns of the north" during his stay in England is incorrect. Windsor, London, Ports- mouth, a fortnight's cruise in his yacht, and. Cowes, are the arrangements in his Majesty's pro- gramme, to which there will certainly be no addi- tion. The Emperor will pay a private visit to the Duke of Edinburgh at Devonport during his cruise down Channel.

Admiral Canevaro, commander of the Venice Arsenal, has arranged that instead of the "Sicilia" being baptised in the usual way, by having a bottle of champagne broken on its bows, the ancient Cus- tom of the Venetian Republic shall be revived. That is, that a gilt ring shall be attached to the vessel's prow in such a way by the godmother that when the ship is launched the ring shall be the first thmg to touch the water, this fulfilling the "wed- ding of the sea."

Each week that passes makes it only too pain- fully plain that the Royal Commission on Labour is aoomed to go the way of all commissions. The process is sadly familiar. First the announcement. with much eclat, of the appointment of the Com- mission. Then the selection of the aristocratically qualified chairman awl his colleagues, some eager and earnest., others listless and unconcerned. Next a few preliminary meetings, whereat much is promised and nothing performed. In the end a report which the long lapse of time has rendered flat, stale, and unprofitable.

Mrs. French Sheldon's African expedition has proved a more serious undertaking than she had anticipated, owing to the unsettled state of some parts of the country. She had intended to have only 50 porters, but. these refused to go without an armed force of at least 70 men. Mrs. Sheldon has therefore been obliged to have a hundred porters, 70 of whom are armed. The cable to the effect that the enterprising lady has started from Kilmanjar for Pangani on the coast indicates that she has turned her face homeward. If all go well, she will be home by the end of July.

A conclusive proof of public sympathy with the orunthils men who are on strike, was afforded on Wednesday night at the great gathering of South St. Pancras Liberals, in the Holborn Town Hall, by the remarkable outburst of cheering which greeted the following words of the Marquis of Ripon: can express no opinion as to the details of the quar- rel, but this I will say—the long hours that omnibus men have had to labour are disereditable to this country. I think, for my part, if it should come to be a question of short hours or high dividends, the dividends must go to the wall."

The new Goethe " Jahrbuck " tells something more than was previously known about Goethe's last days. A letter from Frommann, contributed by Julius Wahle, says, "Goethe, as he had difficulty in breathing while lying, sat, in a ch air on the morning of his death. He was more cheerful than usual, read a book, joked with his daughter-in-law, , Ottilie, telling her to bring her chair closer and Closer, and pressing her hand, which he still held when he died. One of the last things he said was, I 'Give me your dear little paw' " (Notchen). A letter from Jenny von Pappenheim, contributed by her grand-daughter, Lily von Bretschman, says: "He may very likely have spoken the words 'More light! 'but his last words, clear and distinct, were: Now cones the change to higher changes' (Nun kommt die Wandelung zu hoheren Wandelungen). Rly last recollection was the funeral procession which bore him to the Royal vault of Carl August."

div.head: DELIRUM TREMENS SET IN.
div.p: DELIRUM TREMENS SET IN.

Another man and I were placed in the room to watch him. When I think of it now, it almost un- nerves me. What I went through for several days. I could never describe. The screams and yells of a madman, who insisted so long as he could in walk- ing about the room, were fearful. He made several attempts to jump out of the window, several times did the foot passengers force their way into the house in answer to his cries for help, as he said we were murdering him. .At length this passed away, and, helpless, he lay still enough while the arm be- sides him lay swollen almost the size of his body. My work now lay in keeping wet cloths on the arm to keep it cool. At last when the end came I was given a Roman Catholic book—what it was I don't remember—and bid to read the prayers for the dy- ing. At length all was over, and after the long walk to the cemetery,l thought I was free. Not so,li was bound to the heirs, assignees, &c., &c. But, taking the first opportunity, I fled. Taking the train, 1 landed in Warrington on the Christmas eve. Asking my way to Orford lane, I reached the house where Mr. J. Itylands used to live. All beyond looked bleak and desolate, the ground was covered with snow, but I had not forgotten the number, 41, and 1 went on until I found it. A light shone in the window. I knocked at the door. A voice asked "who's there ?" Oh that voice, I knew it well, and gladly I answered —"lt's me, mother,"" Oh, that's our Henry I heard mother say. It was a sorrowful home I made ythat night. Before many days a lawyer's letter came.

div.head: I HAD TO GO BACK.
div.p: I HAD TO GO BACK.

Oh, the misery of that going back. Many a tale could I tell of the life of an indoor apprentice,but I must leave it all. I ran away again, and again my father had to go to Sheffield. This time he came back with the indentures, having paid Me. to have them broken. Two of Warrington's sons, Mr. J. Rylands and Mr. W. Longshaw, helped my father during his endeavours to get me into the wire trade. This was done in spite of the workmen who little knew the anguish they were adding to what my dear old dad was already bearing, ho ended my first con- nection With Sheffield It was years before the faces of those two,theMr. and Mrs., ceased to accompany me to bed,and many a time did I start in my sleep, with her voice ringing in my ears. Do I know any- thing of the drink question?, I think I do, more than most people, and I have often wished I had the power of tongue which would enable me to show, vividly, and in such a fashion that, not only a mute answer, but an active response, would be given to my appeal. Workmen, your greatest enemy is drink, your weakest side is that bounded by drink. More than once have I seen in important meetings, in which I have had to take a leading part, half drunken men second resolutions which they would immediately vote against. More than once have I seen in important committee work touching the wage question, how a timely adjourn-

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.

THELWALL AND LATCFIFORD. A steady progress is being made with the work on the Ship Canal in this district. The ironwork of the girder bridge near the locks now completely spans the canal and presents a most imposing appearance. The stone- work of the locks is now all but completed and during the week workmen have been engaged in building up a pair of gates for the main lock. As before explained,eaoh gate is completed and put together at the workshop at Thelwall, after which it is taken to pieces for transit and put together again in the place where it is finally to swing. The gates themselves, their bedding, and the grooves in which they have to move are altogether fine piecesof work and excite the admiration of all who have seen the gates whilst being placed in positson. The foundation for the swing bridge at Knutsford-road are being pro- ceeded with, and considerable progress has now been made in preparing the sub-way for the new railway station at Latchford, which is to be erected on the em- bankment between Grappenhall-re ad and Wash-lane.

PARTIAL OPENING OF THE CANAL. We understand that the engineers are actively at work at the Eastharp end with a view to getting the canal absolutely finished between Eastham and Ellesmere Port at a very ?arly date. Their object is to fill this section of the canal with water as soon as possible and transfer the traffic of Ellesmere Port into the canal. It is hardly necessary to say that when this is accomplished it will stimulate interest in the canal and faith in it as a com- mercial undertaking. FATAL ACCIDENT AT ACTON GRANGE.

A fatal accident occurred on Sunday night on the Ship Canal works at Acton Grange to John Robert Dean, 33 years of age, an engine driver. It appears that the deceased lett his own engine about eight o'clock to speak to another driver, and on his return the stud of the coun- ter shaft caught his trousers and caused him to fall down a sump, which is about Mt. deep. The accident was witnessed by the fireman on the other engine, who immediately went for assistance. John Hill and J. Thompkins, gangers, descended the sump and brought Dean out, but it was found that life was extinct. The body was removed to the hospital at Latchford. The deceased lived in Chester-row, Wilclerspool. On Thurs- day afternoon, at the Ship Canal Hospital, Mr. H. C. Yates, coroner, held an inquiry touching the dbath of Dean. Abraham Dean, brother of the deceased, gave evidence of identification. JohnTallman, engine driver, stated that the deceased's engine stood alongside his. He knew the deceased's engine belt had broken, and that he was going to repair it. He came to witness's engine and went back overa piece of timber. Witness heard a shout and looking up: caught a glimpse of Dean, falling down the sump. Witness at once stopped his. engine and went down, but the Men was quite dead. John Hill, foreman testified that the-footpath was a dangerous one. He had cautioned Dean-and other men against using it. There was another pathway, but this was one- often taken to save time,. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental .death."

CANAL BILL. IMPORTANT RECOMMENDATIONS.

The Local Government Board have prepared a report upon the Manchester Ship Canal Bill which. is to be laid before the hybrid Committee of the House of Commons, to which the Bill has been referred. In this report the Board state that it does not appear, from the preamble, whether the shareholders have been called on to pay up so much of the share capital as has not been paid up, or whether there are any unpaid calls, or whether any action has been taken for the recovery of the unpaid calls if any, or for the forfeiture of shares on which calls have not been paid up, or for the sale of forfeited shares. Upon these points the Boarctsubmit that the Committee should be furnished with full information. The Board further observe generally that the construetion and'enaintenance of canals and docks are matters not coming within the scope of ordinary duties of local authorities, and that the rapid increase whieh has taken place of late years in the indebtedness of urban authorities and the many calls that have been made upon them are reasons; which, in the opinion of the Board, render it expedient that great caution should be exercised in conferring upon these authorities the power of borrewing money for other pur- poses. Assuming, the report continues, thaa the Commit- tee are satisfied that the case is one in which:it is desirable that the Corporation should come to the assistance of the Company, it is manifestly of the greatesleimportance that every reasonable precaution should be taken for protecting the interests of the ratepayerseand the Board are very doubtful whether these interestsare adequately safeguarded by the • Bill as framed. The Board then proceed to criticise the clauses in great detail: On clause 15 they say :.---" By this clause it is provided that the Corporation shall receive in respect of moneys lent by them to the Company new debenturesto an equal amount in the form set forth in the second schedule to the bill and upon the conditions therein appearing. The , conditions provided for by the form of debenture appear ; to be that all the securities already issued, mete be here- after issued under the Company's existing Acts, shall have priority over the new debentures ;that if the money secured by the newdebentures is not repaid on the Ist of January, 1897, the Company shall pay interest thereon at £4 10s per cent. • ,and that if they -continue to pay such interest the capital shall not be repayame save at their option. The Board are advised that, having regard to these conditions the stipulation hi the debentures that the principahall be repaid to the mortgagee on the let of January, 7.897, cannot be enforced by the Corpora- tion, and that in the event of the Company not deciding to repay the principal the only method,by.whiele the Cor- poration could recover any part of the money advanced would be by selling the debentures._ The effect ot clause 25 in the bill appears, however, to be to prevent the Cor- poration from eelling any debenture except at or above par. It wouldeterefore seem that there will, be little probability of the Corporation recovering any partof the principal proposed to be advanced by thern unless the canal proves such a Commercial success that the Com- pany theinsel-ees desire to pay off , the debentures pro- posed to be i 391.10 under the bill e or unless soch deben- tures, notwiehstandingthat they are postponed to the other loan capital of the Company, ,can. be sold to the public at or-above par. The Board submit for the con sideration of the Committee bether the debentures pri posed to be given to the Corporationunder this clause in,i 'exchange fier the £3.000,000 which the Corporation are to lend to the Company can be.regareled WI satisfactory. securitieeemfficiently safeguarding the interests of the ratepayees, and in connection with, this question they would dmwthe attention of the COmmittee,to the obser- vations on clause 7. It is also, to be observed that the. form of:the neuedebentures provides that if the fe'ttim- pany gives six months' notice to the holder of their , intention to repay the principal secured thereby after r, the lse- of January, 1897; the holder may, instead of , receiving payment of hisprincipal, require the Company to issue to him a perpetual mortgage debenture or per- petual debenture stock in substitution for the new debenture, but carrying a lower rate of interest. The ; Board submit for the consideration of the Committee 'whether it is desirable that any part of the money ad- vanced by the Corporation to the Company should con- tinue so advanced after the Company are witting and in a position to repay the same. In connection with this question it is to be observed that any ultimate profit made by the Corporation under the bill may be handed ;over to the Company under clause 28." On clause 2S the Board remark e--" This, clause as at present drawn is open to many objections. In the first place it imposes no obligation on the Corporation for ten years to establish a sinking fund for the repay-. ment of the dobt created by them under the hill. If . _ _

this debt were created under the general law (see the Public Health Act, 1875, sec. 234, and the Local Loans Act, 1875, sa. 13-15), it would be necessary that pro- vision for its repayment should commence within one year from the date of the borrowing of the money in each case. div.head: ROMANCE OF THE HIGHLANDS.
div.p: A ROMANCE OF THE HIGHLANDS.

A romantic episode in Highland. life is at present exciting a great deal of attention in 'the North. A -,ew months ago a large sheep farmer in Rossshire ! died. lie wasa, man of great wealth, and father, of one daughter of exceedingly gentle and attrac- tive manners.. Exercising her own mind, some years ago,- she married an Established Church minis- term n the-North, who, besides being:a man of con- siderable standing in his own sphere, has made a very creditable appearance in literatore. The mar- riage, however, seems.to have been opposed by the- young lady's-father, who made a will leaving her only a small pittance.. The lady diets, after having given birth to a son.. After her father's death his will was read, and from it it seemed as if his former inflexible attitude towards his daughter had beets maintained: About a week after, however, several persons, including some of the execators, in search- ing the house, opened a cabinet in which a secret drawer was discovered. On the drawer being opened a codicil was found which left all the farmer., money to his daughter's son. This. discovery has. given great satisfaction throughout the North. The.- money to which the youth has now, fallen heir it,; stated at oTer £lOO,OOO.

div.head: PERCIVAL GORDON;
div.p: PERCIVAL GORDON;
OR, THE CHILD OF THE REGIMENT.
BY SYLVANUS COBB.
CHAPTER XV. A THUNDERBOLT FROM A CLEAR SKY.

Tom Crawford heard of Felix McAllister at Exeter, where he was well known to several of the non-commissioned officers at the barracks, as well as to the host of the public-house where the soldiets there stationed most did congregate. McAllister had stopped at the inn—the "Royal Arms"—two days, after which he had gone down the river to Topsham. At Topsham the old sergeant traced his man to the "Crown and Anchor" inn, where he had tarried three days, having left there only two days before, for the purpose, he had declared, of going into Dorsetshire. So eastward Tom took his course, but before pushing on he went a few miles out of his way to report progress at Wenham. Percival, when he knew that his old friend was bound for Dorset, and that he would pass Ehndale on his way, resolved to accompany him, for the earl had distinctly invited him to call if he should ever find it convenient.

So, on a warm, pleasant afternoon in mid-June, Captain Percival Gordon, riding one of Wenham's favourite pacers, alighted- at the foot of the marble steps leading to the broad piazza of Elmdale Man- sion. A servant in waiting took his horse, and Lady Caroline herself was mi the piazza to welcome him.

The servant who had taken the horse, and who had been most agreeably impressed by the looks and the bearing of the young officer—for Percival wore the rich and graceful uniform of the staff— when he reached the stable, exclaimed to his fel- low-servants there assembled :

"Ho I ho I don't let us think any more that our young mistress is cold-hearted and grown up with- out loving. If you could have seen what I just saw—l tell you, lads, the lover has come, and I've seen him; and he's one o' the right sort, too. I wish you could 'a' seen Lady Caroline's face when she met him. My eyes? her face just ihone with the very double-distilled quintessence of heaven's own happiness! That's what it was." Naturally there was a strong desire among the servants after this to see the youthful captAiu ; and when they had learned his name, a few of the older ones remembered the story of the boy hero of the brigands' cavern, and also called to mind the reports in the Lonlon papers of that same boy's subsequent heroism at Waterloo and other places. And when they knew that he was it? love with their beautiful young mistress, how natural it was that they should institute comparison between him and Matthew Egerton; and when it is considered that they loved their gentle, kind-hearted mistress we can readily believe that they felt deeply in her behalf.

- We can judge from the report of the grooni how our hero was received by Lady Caroline, and we must do the earl the credit of confessing that he put away all outward sign of disapprobation in his reception of his visitor. Yet he was resolved, if the young man should remain over night, to have a plain and candid talk with him in the morning. He felt that he could speak with more ease and freedom to one of his own sex than to his beautiful, winsome daughter. For the present he conversed pleasantly while he remained in Percival's com- pany, and when Caroline, late in the afternoon, suggested to him that she would dearly enjoy it to take a saddle ride in Captain Gordon's company, be made no objection. Percival concluded not to put Wenham's 'pacer tO his extra work; so he went out to the otable with Caroline and the earl to make selection from the Elmdale stud. He followed the head groom from stall to stall, chatting pleasantly as he went, pointing out particular points of excellence- that met his eye, and offeringn few very valuable sug- gestions ; but this latter he did so modestly, and with a tact so peculiarly his own, that the grooms were made to feel that he had gathered the hints given from intelligent remarks of their own. And when he came to vault into the saddle, upon the back of a fiery young charger of wonderful beauty and nerve, they were ready to declare, from the bottom of their hearts, that he was the most gallant rider they had ever set eyes upon. And I. even the earl could not dispute them. _

The young couple had been gone but a abort. time when the earl received a visit from his brother, Roland, who came- with signs of treulde- -,upon his face. ' "Bless me ? " cried the- master of the howee, 'bolding his brother's hand in a warm grasp.. "1 though t you had gone fa-Paris." "1 was all ready to go, Dick, with wife. end babies in their best bibs and tuckers, when it-WH.S. told to me how near to his end old Oxton was, and the thought came to me that I ought to come. .and see you. I have been over to Oxton„, and Walter. Buckley is sinking. fast. Now, don't. be alarmed, old fellow, because there may not be the least particle of danger.. But—have yo ever heard anything of a lot of mortgage deeds hold by the Karl of Oxton, and given by the father of; the Earl. of Elrndale, whom you succeeded ? " . "Deeds! Mortgage deeds!" gasped Iliehaed. "What do you mean?" "I imam that Caleb archer, father of Benjamin, when. he was lord of this estate, borrowed vast sums, of Stephen Buckley„ father of the Earl of Oxton. now dying. This Caleb was a reckless spendthrift—a gambler—and given to Tine. and debauchery of every kind. Old Bowles came to me, not long since, and told me the whole story. His father was the notary who made out the papers, and attested ,their. execution. 1 asked Bowles—you remember him as the attoruay, whom I used to employ—kasked4 him why he had came to meat this late day with the story, and he answered that he believed Lady Caroline would :lever con- sent to marry with young Egerton; and he said he- did not blame her; nevertheless, when that gentleman should have-succeeded to thettit3e, and to the estate, and to the documentary property of Oxtott, these same mortgage deeds would come into his. possession, and he would be very likely to make. use of them.

"And now, dear old Dick, if whae I saw half- an-hour or more ago has the significance which I: Was inclined to give it, the situation is iark enough. Who is that gay and handsome officez I saw riding,. with Carrie?
A deep groan burst! from the ensl'a lips as.he started from his chair and crossed the room. He came back and sank into his seat.

"Roland I—these mortgages 1--shat are they,l. Can you tell nit?" "They Are what I have told you, Richard.; mortgages given to, Stephen Buckley, Earl of Oxton, by Caleb Archer, Earl of Elmdalo-; and they cover so much of this property that were they foreclosed, and payment in full enforced, you would ha a penniless peer. Yu would be still Earl of Elmdale, and I should restore to.you the estate of.our family to enable pail° live.!" Richard. Archer was not the man to bear mis- fortune with equanimity. He bent his head upon his hands and groaned in bitterness of spirit. "Saddle your fleetest horse, and ride with all possible speed to Oxton. If the earl haa his senses, and can speak, ask him, frankly, when thwe deeds are, and see if you can make an arrangement with him by which, you can obtain them. Old Murray is his lawyer,, as he is yours, and he will befriend you, if necessary, if he can." Richard reflected for a little time, and then darted up,. resolved to do as his. brother had suggested, and to lose no, time in its accomplish- ment
The distance to Oxton Castle was ten miles. Within an hour from the time. of leaving his library Richard Archer had been ushered into the chamber where lay Walter Buckley, seventh Earl of Oxton.
He found the old man dying. Matthew Egerton bad just arrived, and was below with the steward. He took a seat by the bedside, and asked the earl if he knew him.

Yes, his old friend knew him, but it was with a gasping effort that he spoke. The nurse was in the room, and Richard dared ttot ask her to retire. So he took the dying mates hand and asked him, in a low tone, if he remem- bered certain mortgage deeds given by Caleb Archer to his. father. Walter Buckley 's failing eyes gleamed with a spark of intelligence, and Jae nodded, tried to speak, and lost his breath, where- upon the nurse came forward and forbade further conversation. Then she pushed Elmdale aside and caught up her patient's head, which had sunk low down upon the pillow, and his nether jaw had fallen while a low, gasping, rattling sounti issued from Lis ashen lips. With a smothered groan, Richead Archer left the chamber' and to a servant, whom he met on the landing, he said that the earl was dying. Then he descended the great stairway, and in the lower hall he mot Matthew Egerton. The latter was the first to speak. "Lord Eimdale, what does the visit of that gallant spark from Wenham mean? Why is hti riding out with my promised wife? By the—u

A big, coarse oath had escaped the vulgar lips, when the earl stopped him. "Dear Matthew, do not fly into &passion. You know what that youth is to Caroline. She feels grateful to him. When he called upon us, as I felt in duty bound to invite him to do, my child could not do less than she is doing. Remember, be saved both our lives. But, dear boy, wait. Let us hope that all will be pleasant and agree- able."

Matthew had burst forth with a bitter, vulgar speech against Caroline, when Elinda.le stopped him by informing him that Lord Oxton had, in all probability, breathed his last. "His LAST ? " cried the long-waiting heir. "Do you mean it?" "I do," said the other, solemnly. Matthew Egerton uttered a round oath—an oath such as the fortunate gamester utters—and turned and sprang up the stairs, two steps at a leap. Richard Archer watched him until he had passed from sight, and then, with a bursting sigh, and an expression of unutterable and undefinable emotion upon his still handsome face, he turned and slowly moved, with head bowed, towards the library, where he thought he might gather up his scattered senses without being disturbed. Himself, in that moment, could not have told what feeling was uppermost in his bosons ; whether a great dread of the loss of Elmdale dsmesne, with its long rent roll, and its quarries not to be valued, or a sicken- ing, shuddering, loathing disgust of Matthew Egerton. He reached the library, and there found the old lawyer, James Murray, alone. His first impulse was to withdraw instantly -,; but a moment's reflec- tion; told him that this was the man to answer a few important questions he. had to ask. So he entered, and took a seat. Murray presently looked up-from an old account- hook, the pages of which he had been studying, and pleasantly greeted the new-coiner. Elmdale. was one of his favourite clients, and he also liked the man: Without a word of the dying, or the probable death, of the lord of Oston, Rieliard stoat at the subject that lay nearest his heart,
He swallowed a gl-s of wine at the sideboard; and, having gained control of his thoughts, he resumed his seat, and told to thelamyer the story of his brother's mission._

"It came upon me," he went on,, "like a thun- derbolt from a clear sky. It was the first intima- tion I had ever had ol any such thing. My dear Murray, can you explain it! Tell me the whole truth. Keep nothing back." "My lord," replied the lawyer, with true feel- ing, "your brother did not overstate the case. I can remember both Caleb Archer and Stephen Buckley—Earls of Elendale and of Oxon. 1 waS but a boy, however, when they died; but my father, who was associated with Wallace Bowles, father of the present attorney, Joshua Bowles, had a hand in making the mortgage deeds. In fact, he and Bowles together did it all. The facts are simply these me Earl of Elmdale, Caleb, as • your brother has told you, was given over.to about every social voiee in the calendar. He lost enormous sum at play, and he spent a forttfird on loose characters of'both sexes; for when in, his cups he cared little or nothing for the reputation of his associates, and during the last half of his life he was in his cups continually. Earl Stephen of Oxton, on the contrary, was close and saving, bleb not niggardly, though I have always been of tha opinion that, had he lived, he would have taketa the fair domain of Elmdale to himself. When Caleb Archer wanted money he went to Stephen and got it, giving notes at high rates of interest fidnu thousands,aenvlwet ei lo nfpttothhr thoeeeep aurwa:mnyh dreooent ovngaehat ayrtemsoel •uaoowhrbir oatobtguduhrlatil.al mortgages—.there presenttel reacitiirtgdeeta:oitii ne, esytom_hf (ei tea hant transfer- rablealtko aren take Richard Archer bunied his face in his hand, and • groaned aloud: "My dear Elmdale continued Murray, deeply moved, "I should have made, or attempted to make a movement in, your behalf when you first came to the title, had not a way been opened,, as I clearly thought, for a pleasant settlement of the ' whole business. I allude to the betrothment of - your daughter, and heiress, to the heir of °cotton. 1 spoke of the matter 'with Joshua Bowles, and we both took the same

At this point Murray stopped, as though I:e.sita- ting about speaking as, he had intended to ,apeak, but after a brief pause he went on, though-in, lower tone, and very guardedly: "There was a time, my lord, when Bowie!' ,was

, really contemplating at surreptitious taking away of those papers. it was very evident to n.-bcitli that old Stephen Buckley had passed away without making known to his son theexistence of thosuniart- gage deeds, and we did not believe that the present earl knew of them, though he knows of them now. In fact, during the :years of his sickness he,. has ransomed every nook, hoie' and corner of the. old castle, and critically examined every paper found. However, as I was saying, Bowles was already tempted to purloin those deeds. That was thirteen years ago, and,little more, when he fancied that your brother -.might succeed, you- being thought dead, away off in Spain.-Lees -the recollection of the grim- ordeal pain yon.letillr ".No, no, not that, Murray. It was another thought. Go on. Did Bowles make any move- ment in that direction ?"

"No. Before he had arranged a plan youput in an appearance, an& be had nothing more to do in Roland's behalf. And now tell me, if you will: Is it settled that Laay Caroline will not- become Egerton's wife ?" A. look of pain swept over the earl's Zees* and he said: "Mr. Murray, ,answer me this: Red you daughter of Caroline's age whom you laved as yeti loved your own lifst—"'
The lawyer put forth his hand, andtintorruptea
". I have such ik-.4langhter."

"Yes—l know:. She is Caroline'sdriend. You can answer me, it aeeins, from the heart. Would you give, freely and willingly, the hand •ed your child to Matthew. Egerton ?" "My dear Eluidaie, you and I -cannot answer that question from, the same standpoint. Remenr ber—your estate is at stake. If thimman is refused the hand of his,atfianced wife, he ill surely corne upon your est. 'a.A.for the entire satisfactioa of those mortgages. I have given my word to the Earl of Oxton that I will explain to his heir -the nature of those deeds, and see that they arcteettled upon his bride. That word I must keep.. The result you can foresee. I. am not handicapped. by any such unfortunate impediment." "I did not ask you what you-, would do if you' were in my place," said the earl,, almost sternly 3, "but I appealed to your father's heart." "But, my lord, you have, with your own hand,. signed the-.deed of betrothment."- " That, in England, cannot- force the din& against hr, will. Would you. attempt to exercise. your parental will against your child's earnest,- prayer for.release ? If you hares.. thought of yoisr own, letme. have an answer.."' "Then, .my. lord, plainly,, frankly and emphs,i- eally—No l I could not find; it. in my heart t0,40,- any such thing." " Nor can L So let the men dolls worst. An, now, Mr. Murry, you had bettor go up to. lordship'achs.mber. I think he. has breathed. WO last."•

Whereupon the old lawyer,, without anotbet word, hurried away, nthile the Earl of Eluvial° found his hat and gloves, and called for his horse. An hour later he wanwith kis brother in his olf° library. "Hush!" he said, when ha had told the story" his mission,—and he had omitted nothing,—.. let the matter rest for now. I will only say.,—l have seen that to-day in Matthew Egerton which has filled my cup of disgust. to overflowing. Bette poverty than the misery of such degradation! will, not even speak with Caroline on the subject' Her young life shall, not be clouded by zalamity prospect. Let the worst come, and I will meet it. Dear Roland, I shell not, under any circumstances* take back from you that which I freely gave. 13111 should my cherub, become the wife of the man ° he; choice, I may, for a little time, ask a 1100 beneath your roof. ti "Dick I Bless your noble, generous heart, have is yours ; take what you. will, and take when you will." "Enough. Ah ! here comes Caroline—and bl gallanp captain with her. Two short hours ago did not think I should ever smile upm their love; but now, though the cost may be the fall fro: affluence to poverty, I can do it with all my hOrsh And do you know, my brother, I feel a woo' a about my heart in the shadow of this threate°_,e calamity which I have not felt before for a low long thus.'

ANOTHER VICTIM OF THE HOWLEY
DEATH-TRAP. A SCORE OF CHILDREN PREVIOUSLY DROWNED THERE.

1 An inquest was held by Mr. S. Brighouse, , 'coroner, in the Parade Room of the Police Court, on I Monday morning, concerning the death of John Norton, aged three years, son of Patrick Norton, labourer, Lord Nelson-st., who was drowned in I Howley Brook, yesterday afternoon week, as pre- viously recorded. The first witness called was the deceased's mother. She said she last saw him alive on Friday, and he was brought home dead within a quarter of an hour. The children in the neighbourhood all made for the vacant piece of land (through which the brook flows) to play. The grandfather of a child who was playing with the deceased at the brook said the lads were swimming corks, when the deceased overbalanced himself and fell in. Jehn Hayes, Napier-st.. said he was getting his dinner When be heard screams. On going outside lie heard that the child was under the culvert, and he got into the water. There was a grid about a yard under the culvert, and the deceased could not go through. He pulledtbe child out and conveyed it home. There was about 2ft. of water in the brook. The coroner referred to the fact that certain recommendations had been made at previous inquests to the Corporation, and suggested that it would be advisable for the jury to ask the town-clerk and borough surveyor, who were both present, as to what had been done.—Mr. S. Davies, fore- man of the jury, said he did not see it was worth while to make any recommennation or say anything more in the matter. He did not see that anything had been done. The Town-clerk said no legal responsibility could be laid at the door of the Corporation, who had done all they could in the matter of improving the condition of the brook and putting it in a safer condition. But the Cor- poration could do nothing unless they got the consent of the landowners. The Corporation sought last year an extension of their boundaries, and they endeavoured to get the whole of the Tvryste's brook within the borough. They did not want to close their eyes to their moral re- sponsibility, and they had endeavoured to deal with the closing of the brook. By an ingenious contrivance the tidal water from the river-had been prevented from flow- ing up the brook, and a grid had been placed at the mouth Of the culvert to prevent children being carried under, but the force of the water must have carried it under. They had gone to a considerable expense in dealing with that portion of the brook within the borough, and that although there Was no legal responsi- bility attaching to them. Correspondence had taken place between the Corporation and the owners through whose land the brook passed, and all but three had con- sented to the Corporation dealing with the matter.— The Coroner inquired whether the three who were stand- ing out were large owners, and what their objection was. Personally, he thought if the brook were closed up the owner would have a better frontage to his land.—The Towri Clerk said that was the argument the Corporation put forward, but the owner could not see it.—The Coroner : Suppose these men gave way, what scheme would you propose? The Town Clerk said they wanted to make it into a sewer, which would go through the middle of a supposed street. They had been engaged in banking up the brook to prevent flood water swelling in, • and they had to ask the consent of the landowners to do this. Colonel Blackburne was providing the labour and the Corporation found the material.—The Coroner asked how they could get the brook filled up by the houses.—The Borough Surveyor said it would cost £9,000 or £lO,OOO to provide for the flood waters, and only £1,500 to deal with it as a sewer.—The Town-clerk said the Corporation ,were absolutely powerless unless the landowners gave their consent.—The Coroner said it was a lamentable thing that children should be losing their lives in this death-trap, but at the same time they could not help but see that there were a great many difficulties in the way of the Corporation. It appeared to him that what the officials stated was correct, the Corporation were not failing in their duty.—The Fore- man said he did not wish to use any strong language, but it was a little less than a disgrace that this death- trap should be allowed to exist in so populous a district as Howley was. Perhaps those responsible would state how many lives they wanted sacrificing, before.steps were taken to cover the brook in. He recol- lected some twenty children being drowned in the brook, and several cases bad occurred during the last two years. The Coroner hinted that perhaps the Corporation had asked the owners to make a new street, and that this stood in the way. If the Corporation approached the owners and offered to pay the greater part of the cost it would remove the difficulty. The Surveyor replied that the owners were not asked to construct the street, but simply to lay it out. One owner wished to make a street, but could not do so because a 40ft. street could not be made. If the brook were filled in as proposed a 40ft. street could be made. The Town Clerk assured the court that the Corporation were doing all they possibly could. In reply to further observations the Surveyor said he was surprised to hear of the state of the grid, and he would at once see it was put at the mouth of the culvert. The jury then returned a verdict of "Acci- dental death."
THE CORPORATION PUSHING ON WITH THE
WORK.

We understand that since the inquest, the work of raising the banks of Padgate brook has proceeded very satisfactorily, as also the work of the Ship Canal Com- pany in the widening and re-arching of the outlet into the Mersey. The probability is that in the course of a few weeks operations will be finished which, it is hoped, will prevent any further flooding of Howley district. The Paving and Sewerage Committee havegivon instruc- tions to the Borough Surveyor to obtain tenders for the covaring of the brook down Howley-lane.
THE WHITECROSS WARD CONTEST.
THE NOMINATIONS.

The time for receiving nomination closed on Monday afternoon, when three nomination papers in favour of Mr. Plumpton and two for Mr. Woods had been placed in the hands of the Town Clerk. In one paper Mr. Plump- ton is nominated by Mr. G. Legge, seconded by Mr. I. Hayward, and assented by Messrs. G. Evans, G. Sambrook, B. Shearer, S. Jones, T. Dale, T. Hawthorn, W. Brough, and J. Lloyd. In a second paper he is nom- inated by Mr. J. Salt, seconded by Councillor F. W. Monks, and assented to by Messrs. W. Throssell, T. Hol- lingsworth, J. Evans, A. H. Rathbone, J. A. Heywood, J. Tildsley, C. Longshaw, and G. Hassal. In the third paper Mr. Plimpton is nominatid by Councillor S. J. Beaman, seconded by Mr. R. Roscoe, and assented to by Messrs. A. H. Dunn, W. Hardy, J. Fieldhouse, J. W. Hayward, B. Percival, W. Crosskill, W. Wright, and J. T. Bradbury. Mr. Woods, in one paper is nominated by Councillor Linnteus Greening, seconded by Mr. H. W. Cookson, and assented to by Messrs. J. Battersby., J. Thornton, junr., J. Eaton, J. Kean, S. Hill, D. 'lams, R. Hatton, and J. Dutton. In a second paper he is nominated by Mr. R. T. Smith, seconded by Mr. J. Houghton, and assented to by Messrs. H. Houghton, W. Needham, W. H. Bellian, W. Alden, J. Parkinson, W. Bellian, W. J. Potter, and S. Rustage. ENTHUSIASTIC LIBERAL MEETING. MR.

hear, and applause.) Something had been said by the Tories about his being a Liberal Unionist. Wel„ he did not know what a Liberal Unionist was himself; he had never thought so much about it. If they callest him Liberal Unionist he did not object to it, and if they called him Radical he did not object to that. (Hear,hear,) He knew there was one thing they would not call him, and that was a Conservative. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) lie was in favour of the greatest Radical reforms, and he had never voted for a Conservative at either municipal or Parliamentary elections, and he had never abstained from voting for a Liberal candidate when he had been in the town or could be in the town. (Ap- plause,) He was in favour of Home Rule for England, Ireland, Scot/and and Wales, and he was in favour of the abolition of the House of Lords altogether. (Laughter and applause.) He believed that when Mr. Gladstone again came into power he would bring in a Home Rule bill that would suit him. (Hear, hear and applause.) Mr. Plumpten next Spoke in favour of the improvement and enlargement of the baths, and of the provision of a Turkish bath. He also thought that on certain days of the week there ought to be cheap rates charged, S. that no one should be precluded the benefits of the baths by the highness of the charges. (Hear, hear.) Speaking with regard to the gas he was in favour of a reduction.! the price, and the meter rents being either reduced or abolished. (Applause, and a voice "Abolished.") As te Longford depots he did not know whether he should agree altogether with their chairman, and if he (the chairman) brought anything forward in the Council he could not support he would not vote for him. (Hear, hear and laughter.) He was of opinion that something ought to be done with the intercepting depots and Longford works. There was no mistake about it that other people could smell them besides those living in their immediate neighbourhood. There ought, at events, to be no objection to a public inquiry. Tue- ratepayers surely had a right to ask ;how their money was being spent, without its being considered an in- fringement of the dignity of or the confidence in the _ .

Sanitary Committee-or any other Committee. (Hear, hear and applause.) With regard to the dwellings in the town, he had heard that there were some which were not fit for a dog Lc. live in. (Hear, hear, and "Quite true.") If that were true how could the Town Council consider it was doing its duty by allowing these things to exist. (A Voice: "Self-interest.") That was true ;it was because there were members of the Town Council interested in that property. (Hear hear.) What did the property owners agent care so long as he got his , rents, but he said "shame" on the men who had the duty of looking after such places and yet allowed theta to exist. (Loud applause.) The speaker concluded amidst hearty applause by saying that he had every confidence in being returned by a large majority. The CHAIRMAY thought the speech Mr. Plumpton mad* that night justified their choice of a candidate. (Hear, hear.) He was glad to hear Mr. Plumpton say that ha- would vote even against him (the Chairman) if he pro- posed what he did not agree with. There were in this town sadly too few men who would stand up in defence of the principles they professed to believe in. (Hear, hear.) Mr. T. Monms then proposed a vote of thanks to th* Chairman for presiding. He had heard their candidate make two speeches now, and he should say that there was not one man in six who had gene into the Council Cham- ber during the last twenty years who could speak his thoughts in the intelligent manner Mr. Plumpton had, done. (Hear, hear.)

CounCillor BEfratiw, in seconding the vote of thanks, referred to the criticisms of the Sanitary Committee. Ele said the Sanitary Committee reminded him of a fine win— dow in St. Pauls Cathedral. From the outside it looked like a chaotic mass of colours, but when they saw it from tht inside its beauty silenced all cavilling. (Laugh- ter and applause.) _ _ _
The mOtion was then carried, and the Chairman having responded, the meeting terminated. CONSERVATIVE MEETING—MR. WOODS'S ADDRESS.

On Wednesday evening a well-attended meeting was held in St. Barnabas School in support of Mr. Alfred Woods, the -Conservative candidate. Coun- cillor Linnmus Greening presided, and there were also present Aldermen Sutton, Wright, Greensll ; Councillors Muir, Hill. Hutchinson Cannell, and Bolton; Messrs. R. Piorpoint, H. W. Cookson, and others.

The OLIIIMAN said he should like to call attention to one point, which was that that seat was their seat until November Ist, and he disapproved very strongly of the policy of grab of their opponents. He thought they might decently have let them nominate a successor to Councillor Greenall, but if the Conservatives put their shoulder to the wheel they would show that the ward was not so hopelessly Liberal as they had been told. (Hear, hear and applause.) Mr. H. W. Cooxsom then submitted apologies for non- attendance from Mr. W. Milner, Mr. J. White, and Mr. W. Carson.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 13, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 13, 1891.
THE EDUCATION BILL.

EXPLANATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS. On Monday, in the House of Commons, the house went into committee on a financial resolution *which it was necessary to pass as the basis of the Assisted Education Bill. Sir William Hart-Dyke said it was his duty to place before the house the proposals yf the Government with regard to relieving parents from the payment of foes in elementary schools. He acknowledged the work that voluntary schools had done in the past, and said that the Government had come to the conclusion that the only possible basis on which to rest ascheme for the settlement of the question would be to give a fee of 10s. per head for each scholar in average attendance in ele- mentary schools. That would be found to be approxi- mately a 3d. fee. The Government proposed that when this grant of 10s. was given to the managers of a school and accepted by the school., and the fees received since the Ist January,lB9l, did not exceed 105. per head per child in average attendance, in every case it should be called a free school. The Government had de- cided to have no standard limitation whatever, but they considered that the grant should be made payable only on behalf of those children of compulsory school age, and that compulsory attendance should be between the age of five and fourteen years. Under five years of age the fee should in no case exceed 241. per head, and this would make a difference of .something like £115,000 from a financial point of -view. As to the application of the-grant to schools, the• Government had come to the condusion to allow any school to receive this free grant of 10s., and to allow a-school where fees were-charged -above the fee grant still to 'receive the grant and receive the balance of fees. Undeilthese pro- posals a sd. school would become al'd. fee school. The Government 'shed to maintain all.classes of schools in the position they now sOod, and where the demand exisbed there would be -free schools or 'free places in certain schools. They proposed thatthe fee grant should be paid quarterly, and after 'eareful calculation they found that -the sum required would be 'rather under than over the sum indicated ;by the Chancellor of the Exchequer. Whenever necessary the Government pro- posed to require that public scheOls should be provided 'without payment of any fee. Mr. Howorth said he and many others could not give very 'hearty welcome to the iproposals of the Govern- ment. tie had both during and-since tho general elec- tion opposed free education, and he now failed to find rany reason or justification forrthe *violent change which was-now proposed. He desired to enter his protest against this form of collectivesocialism, which none of therritiked and some of them -dreaded. Mr. Mundella said even alrthe limitations which the right ton. gentleman oppoilte proposed carried with themthe seeds of death, and they must-soon be swept away. After the speech of that evening he was satisfied that.they were now within the measurable distance of universal free education. As he (Mr Mundella) under- stood the proposal of the 'Government, where the tax had been lightest, these would be.so to speak, the largest grant ; where it had been most oppressive there the oppressive tax would be partly ccntinued. In Lance- 'shire and Cheshire there were-schools where the fees were nearly 195., and in these schools it was obvious that 95. .per head would still be levied on the scholars. Was that free education /1 *Opposition cheers.) Sir William Harcourt assured the Government they would find supporters-of free education on the Opposi- tion benches. What the Opposition wanted was real free education, unrestricted free education, undiluted free education.

Mr. J. Chamberlain supported the Government scheme and said it had ecome a sociatand educational necessity to release the parents of children at •elementary schools from the paymeht of 'fees. •If the eclucatios under the Bill was to be complete, then they should be thoroughly satisfied with the Government measure. He contended it was complete, but he pleaded that the grant should be extended beyond the age of 14 years. After long debate, Mr. W. H. Smith appealed to the House to allow the resolution to be introduced. The resolution was then agreed Wand reported to the House. Although the main reinciple of the Assisted Education Bill meets with almost general acceptanee,its details pro- voke opposition. In more thanone quarter of the House of Commons there was on Monday night less expecta- tion than ever that the measure, with.all the rest of the Ministerial programme, can be carried through by the end of July, when Ministers hope to be able to prorogue Parliament. There is a growing expectation in the House, that, after having past its early stages, the Edu- cation Bill win be remitted to a winter,session.

div.head: TEXT OF TEIE BILL.
div.p: TEXT OF TEIE BILL.

A London correspondent says :—The text of the bill issued on Tuesday nightis'being eagerly studied on both sides of the House. Thereare one or two points which did not arise in Sir W. Hart-Dyke's speech, but are to be found in the bill itself, on which explanations will cer- tainly be askedfor. Thus, for instance, the third clause, which the Vice-President failed to touch upon on Mon- day night, enables the Eduzation Department to ap- prove the raising of fees in schools to Which the grant has been made when this•course is considered to be for the benefit of the district. ,It was certainly not under- stood that such a proposal.was contained in the bill,and it will meet with much 'opposition unless accompanied by very strict limitations. Another prefectly absurd provision is clause ?,which provides that the word "fee" shall include any profit made by the managers or teachers of the school on the sale of books or other articles supplied to the children. This provision simply puts a premium on extravagant charges for books and other school paraphernalia, and it will certainly have to be abandoned. A question has been raised; too, as to the position of schools which have:raised the fees this year, say, front threepence to fourpence. Apparently, by the powers of the bill, they will be made perfectly free, although the fee may have been raised in eonse- quence of improved educational aarangements, as the second clause provides that the estimate of the revenues of the school is to be based on the fees taken in the twelve months previously to January lof this year. A school which had throughout charged fourpence without making any improvements would, on the other hand, be , entitled to continue to charge one penny.

The annual meeting in connection with the National Reform Union was held on Wednesday in Liverpool. The General Council met in the afternoon to adopt the report and transact other business of a formal character. Speeches were made by Sir Wilfrid Lawson, M.P., Mr. C. E. Schwann, M.P. (who was re-elected president of the Union), Mr. T. D. Sullivan, M.P., and others. In the evening there were two public demonstrations, at which the chief speakers were Mr. Campbell-Bannerman, M.P., Sir Edward Grey, M.P., and Sir Wilfrid Lawson, M.P.

div.head: PLUMPTON'S ADDRESS.
div.p: PLUMPTON'S ADDRESS.

A very largely attended meeting was held on Monday evening, in St. Barnabas Schools, Warring- ton, in support of the candidature of the Liberal candidate, Mr. George Plumpton, for the vacancy in the representation of the Whitecross Ward on the Town Council. Councillor H. Roberts presided, and he was supported by Councillors W. Pierpoint, J. H. Fleming. J. Shaw Green, T. Flood, S. J. Ben- man; Messrs. T. Morris, T. Birchall, G. Legge, J. Walker, I. Heyward, J. Salt and others. The pro- ceedings throughout were marked by confidence and enthusiasm.

The CHAIRMAN, in opening the proceedings, referred to the charge by the Conservatives that the Liberals were causing the expense of that contest, and pointed out that a few months ago, when Alderman Platt was elected to be an alderman, the Conservatives contested a seat which had for many years been a Liberal seat. They won it, too, but the Liberals were going to do exactly the same on that occasion. (Applause.) He had heard it objected against Mr. Plumpton that he was not an educated man,but he had said, look around the present 1 Town Council and pick out the educated men and he was afraid they would find them in a hopeless minority. But, besides, was the want of education in a man's early days to be a bar against his rising? He thought it was to Mr. Plumpton's credit if he had overcome those difficul- ties and made himself a success to-day. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. Plumpton had also been objected to be- cause he was a Liberal-Unionist, but he (the Chairman) certainly did not expect to see the time when the Tories would oppose a man on the ground that he was a Liberal- Unionist. (Hear, hear.) He asked for their support of Mr. Plumpton on the ground that he was a fit man to represent them, that he was a large ratepayer who went in and out amongst them, and, being a neighbour, they knew all about him. (Applause.) Mr. G. LEGGE moved a resdution declaring Mr. Plump- ton to be a fit and proper person to represent the Ward, and pledging the meeting to use every legitimate means to secure his return. (Applause.) Mr. A. H. Dumq seconded this proposal. He said he believed Mr. Plumpton was the best man before the constituency. Remembering the traditions of their party as a party of progress, he thought that Mr. Plump- ton, as a Liberal, was more adapted to work for the benefit of the town and the ratepayers at large than a Conservative was. (Applause.) Mr. T. BIRCHALL supported the motion, and said that good business men were required in the Town Council. Men who had learnt how to spend their own money, and to spend it carefully, were more likely to spend wisely the money of their fellow-townsmen. (Hear, hear, and applause.) There was no doubt that the present was a political fight, and their opponents were at their old time-honoured, or time-dishonoured tricks. One of the tricks was to bring in the names of people who were likely to exercise an influence in the election. Thanks; however, to the Liberal party, they had a free press. They could read their newspapers; they could study political and municipal questions, and they were able to judge for themselves, and to vote accordingly. In the old times the squire was trotted out in the village and the" common folk were expected to follow suit, which.h ever side he went. Now, thanks to the freedom which had been obtained for them by the Liberal party, Englishmen were able to think for themselves, and to act accordingly. (Applause.) Mr. SALT, who was received with applause, supported the motion, and said that Mr. Plumpton, in his opinion, was a very business-like man, and a man who was fitted in every respect for the position of the representative of the inhabitants of Whitecross Ward. He had been a working-man himself, and, therefore, knew the princi- ples of the working-men with whom he would come into contact. He (Mr. Plumpton) had always had a desire to see the working-man rise, and be properly represented as they should be, and he (Mr. Salt) knew that he would not change his opinion. Years ago as a workman he had benefited the working-men in no small degree by helping to form a Union which represented the working-men and their rights. He (Mr. Plumpton) was now an employer. He was no " sweater," as many people had asserted ,but acted as fairly and generously as a master could. He aTuhsee . r concluded by asking the audience to do their utmost in pl order to return Mr. Plumpton at the election. (Ap- Loluiion was then put to the meeting, and was unanimously and heartily agreed to.

Mr. GEORGE PLUMPTON was received with loud ap- plause and the cry "Our future representative." He thanked them for passing the resolution in so unanimous a manner, and said that if he were returned as member for that ward he would try to discharge his duties so that they would not have cause to regret their choice. It was the first time he had ever attempted to come for- ward as a candidate for municipal honours, and if there was any honour in being a member of the Town Council it was in doing service to their fellow-men. It was for that purpose only that he stood before them that evening. ' (Applause.) He might say that he had no intention of going to the Council before Mr. Hayward, Mr. G. Legge and Mr. Salt, as representatives of Dallam Forge and Whitecross Works, asked him to allow his name to be put forward as a candidate for the Whitecross Ward. After some hesitation he agreed that his name should be put before the Liberal general council of the ward, and shortly afterwards he was told that he had been selected. (Hear, hear.) He was rather surprised the Tory party again brought a candidate into that ward so soon after the beating they had on the last occasion. He was surprised that they should think they could plant a minority candidate amongst a majority of Liberals, such hard-handed working Liberals as they were in the Whitecross Ward. (Hear, hear.) They charged the Liberals with being the cause of the expense of the contest, but he said it was the Conservatives who were causing the expense to the`town. Were the Liberals to allow the Conservatives to make aldermen out of their councillors and then put other councillors in their place? The Conservatives might well have a majority in the Council. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) But if the Liberals won that election the Liberals would have a majority in the Council—(" Of Councillors ")—Yes, with the exception of the Aldermen. He was not going to forget the aldermen. (Laughter.) He thought too much about the aldermen, and his only regret was that they had not to appear before the ratepayers. (Loud applause.) The aldermen were not representatives of the ratepayers ; they were something like the House of Lords. (Hear, hear.) Having been chosen he would fight, and no stone would be left unturned by him for in- creasing the Trialerity secured last November by their Chairman. The Tories said they would fight them again in November, but that would not frighten them (the Liberals) from that contest. They would fight them again in November and beat them again. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Some charges had been brought against him as an employer, and some people were talking about " blacklegs," " knobsticks," and saying he was a sweat- er. He said that no falser charge than that could pos- sibly be made, and no greater insult could be brought against him than that charge. (Hear, hear). (Applause.) He also told the men where the' could get their steel at a much less price than they haa been paying to the masters, and this led the masters to reduce the prices they were charging. At the same time he must say that workmen in his trade were to-day re- ceiving less money than in any other skilled labour. He knew what he had done as a workingman for the work- ing-mon, but he was still as anxious to do what he could for them now that he was a master. (Applause.)
