div.head: BACCARAT SCANDAL.
div.p: THE BACCARAT SCANDAL.

On ltiondarthe jury in the baccarat case were engaged in hearing the concluding speeches of counsel. Sir Charles Russell, for the clefendants,contended that many different acts of cheating had been proved against the plaintiff.; and he relied specially on the " undertaking " to show.that the plaintiff himself hau admitted his guilt. Sir E. Clerk, the Solicitor-General, in the course of an elaborate 'review of the case, urged the importance of various contradictions which had been elicited between the witnesses for the defence, tte,commented strongly on the assertion that the plaintiff had endeavoured to " slip • out of the army onhalf pay.," and said that if Sir W. Gnrdon Cumming's name were remqved from the Army. List it would be impossible t• retain the names of the Prince of Wales and General Williams. The Solici- tor, General cencluded an impassioned appeal, which evoked loud cheers, by asking the jury to believe that in signing the document which the defendants produced, Sir W. Gordon Cumming hallbeen moved by a desire to prevent scandal from attacking the Prince of Wales.

TUESDAY.—VERDICT FOR THE DEFENDANTS. The Chief Justice summed up on Tuesday. Before his Lordship began, General .Owen Williams attempted to make a statement in reply to the Solicitor General's ac- cusation on the previous dayl but was stopped by the Judge. In the course of the summing up the Chief 'Justice gave the Solicitor General an opportunity. of which he availed himself; te say that he unfeignedly re- gretted—and it was thectilv part of his speech he did regret—having said that Lord Coventry and vGeneral Williams had been" falsefriends "tO the plaintiff. He did not intend to use thevords in the sense thatliad been :put upon them. The Chief Juspice went through the evidence at great length. He dwelt on the importance of the fatal undertaking," and asked if it was such a, docutnent as an innocentornan would have signed. With regard to the theory that he signed it in order to protect, the Prince,the Chief Justice said if the Prince had the mis= fortune to sit ata table with a man who had teen guilty of foul play how could 'lt have affected hinit? ' A man might accept death but not dishonour. Could the jury believe a man perfectlyiinnocent would allow himself to put his name to a dishonouring document, ton'document which in effect said that he had cheated and taken money out of the pocket of the Prince of Was by a card- sharping trick, simplythat the world might not know that the Princeof Whles had played baccarat at "Tranby Croft for very moderate stakes? Was not the conse- quence, he asked, far too great for the cause'? Was it not putting an incredible weight upon a gentleman in any circumstances thdt he should allow-himself to be called a card-sbarper and cheat for the rent of Millie for fear that certain actions of the Prince of Wales might be criticised? He hoped that in passingtheir judgment upon Sir Williani's honour they would not be unmindful of their own. His Lordship concluded at twenty-two minutes past three, and the 'prrimmediately retiredto consider their verdict.—The jury returned into court at twenty-two minutes to four o'clo&, and stated they had arrived at a decision.—The Clerk then said : Gentlemen' do you find for the plaintiff oriel. the defendants-?—Thd *Foreman : We find for the defendants (hisses, which vreresuppressed by the usher's crying " Silence.")—Sir.C. ' Russkl : Will your Lordship give,judgment ?—His 'Lordship= In ac- cordance with the verdict.—As the jury left the box hisses again proceeded from the gallery at the 'back of the court.—His Lordship then rose, and the ,public dis- persed.--Some of the defendants as they left were fol- lowed along the corridor by a number of persons, who groaned and hissedifor some time. They tookrefuge in one of the Chancery Courts and subsequently Heft by a side entrance.

INTERVIEW WITH A JURYMAN. A Press representative interviewed.cme of thejtnymen Immediately helefttbe court. He stated that there was no doubt from the first moment thojury entered the pri- vate room how thekverdict would go. As etch juryman was asked whetherhe was for the plaintiff or.the deen- ants, the reply was.unhesitatingly given for the defen- dants. One of the jury, who sympathiski witla. the plaintiff,wasstruck.with the unanimity which prevailed, and, although he would have liked to find for the plain- tiff, he could not conscientiously do so in face of the evi deuce. It appearedto him the jury had made up their minds before the summing up of the Lord Chief Justice.

The Secretary for 'War will shortly be asked ji the House of Commons What action the Commander-in-. Chief proposes to take with-regard to the position in whicl the verdictin the baccarat case leaves the plaintffl., Sir Wm. Gordon Cumming. The subject will also be raised iii the discussion upon the Amy estimates, when one or two members.propose to make some references to the posi- tion of the Prince of Wales with reference to the cas e. A declaration against baccarat was being handed tour td in the Parliamentary lobby on Tuesday for sigraturoi by members of 'Parliament. At the annual meeting of the Carnarvonshire Bar Wet Association, on Tuesday, a resolution was adopted ex- pressing regret that theTrince of Wales wasin the h a.bit of playing cards and gambling, thus lending his sup nirt to immoral practices among the people. :kmeetingwas held at Exeter Hall, on Tuesday nig ht, .under the auspices of the Methodist body, with a vi ow to put an end to the evils of gambling, and, Ag afi rst step,to erect a chapel at Newmarkst. Alderman Mund ell presided. Mr. H. A. Stnith said they ought to ar-ysortie- thing about the gambling in Capel-eourt and Minein lane, and sooner or later they would have to appeal to the Legislature. Sir W.:Gerdon Cumming has resigned his membershi p of all the clubs to which he belonged in London. It is expected that he will now spend the greater part of hi time on his property in the North of Scotland, and lead' the life of a country gentleman. He will, of course, be .cashiered from the Army, and expelled from his clubs' - but in the active pursuits of a landlord he may do much i to retrieve his character and secure that local respect which is some compensation for the lose of" satiety." EHe has always been popular in the North, but hitherto he has not spent much of his timezn his property.

div.head: MARRIAGE OF SIR W. GORDON-- CUMMING.
div.p: MARRIAGE OF SIR W. GORDON-- CUMMING.

-Sir William. Gordon-Cumming was married by special licence on Wednesday morning, at Holy Trinity Church, Sioane-st., London, to Miss Florence Josephine Garner, of ;New York. In consequence of-the secrecy whichhad been observed with regard to the arrangements, there were very few spectators, and the -ceremony was of the simplest character. There were nobridesmaids, but the bridegroom was:aocompanied by Major Vesev-Dawson, of the Coldstream Guards, as best men. The bride, who was accornpanied to the church by Lord Thurlow and: Lady- :Middleton, Sir William Gordon-Cumming's sister,: wore a plain walking dress of Breneh-grey coth and a: black -straw hat, and carried her gloves in her hand: The -00Iciating clergyman was the 11ev. Mr. Walker,' seniorourate of Holy Trinity. the first part of the ceremony, which took place in the Morning Chapel, was performed at theg.ltar steps, and the second at the altar rails. Throughout the ceremony the bride,who was given away by .Lord-Tburlow, :was wreathed in smiles. The register was signed, in addition to the contracting parties, by .Lord ind Lady Middleton, Lord Thurlow, and MaijorAressey.Dawson. Upon leaving the church the bridal party drove to Lord Middleton's residence for the wedding. breakfast. Early in the afternoon Sir William and Lady •Gordon-Cumraing left London for Wollaton Hall, Nottinghamshire, the seat of Lord Middleton. They will remain there untii theend of the week, when they will go to Sir William's Seat in Scotland, where they pro- pose in future to reside. It is stated that after the judg- ment had been given on Moaday,Sir William called upon his fiancee andLoffered to break off the engagement, but she would not listen to the proposal, and ineisted that the ceremony should take place this morning. The lady who is now Lady Gordon Cumming is one of three American sisters. Their father was the head of garner and Co.. a great business house in New York. He was president of the New York Yachting Club, and while holding the office was drowned by the overturning of his yacht fifteen years ago. Clis wife; who was aunt of the present Lady Vernon went down with him, as did all onboard except one lady and gentleman. The girls were looked after by Lady Vernon's mother, and for many years have divided their time between London and Pau. They have a substantial interest in the New York firm. One of them was married at Pau three mouths ago to the Marquis de Breteuil, a semi-semite, who is vastly wealthy, but twenty years her senior. THE HOME OF GORDON CUMMING.

A writer in the "Pall Mall Gazette " says :"—ln the fertile region of Elginshire, known as the Latch of Moray, and along the picturesque shore of Loch Ness, there was a goodly number of people who were watch- ing, with an interest as keen as that of Landon Society, the unique case which has just ended in the Law Courts. In both these districts in the North the name of Gordon Cumming is associated with all that is chivalrous, heroic, and daring. In the first mentioned district Altyre House, near Forres, was known in Sir William's young days as the home of hospitality and good cheer:; and Sir Alexander Penrose Gordon Cumming, the present baronet's father, from his charitable deeds and court- eous manners to all and sundry was one of the most popular of country gentlemen. Not since his death, over twenty years ago, now had the Elgin Volunteers had a lieutenant-colonel as popular as Sir Alexander, and his funeral cortege composed of volunteers, tenantry, and all sorts and conditions of country folk, to the ancient burial. place of the family, at Gordonstoun, some five miles from Elgin, is still re- ferred to as a memorable spectacle. It was at Fort Augustus, at,the head of Loch Ness, that Rowalyn Gor- don-Cumming, a famous kinsman of Sir William's, spent his last days. Of herculean physique, noble and com- manding in appearance,courageous and daring,Rowalyn, from mere love of adventure, proceeded to Africa at a, period when the appellation Dark Continent was much more applicable than it is to-day. - The volume of travel and O,4YVAtUre Vilgeb &waives prowess as a lion-

div.head: -REVOLUTION IN HA.YTI.
div.p: THE -REVOLUTION IN HA.YTI.

EXEOUTIONS AND ASSASSINATIONS. From intelligence which has been received inVew York from,Fort-au-Frince, dated the 31st of last month, it appears that for two or three weeks it has been whis- pered•that a revolutien was being plotted against,Genl. Hypolyte's Government. Oirthese rumours coming to the ears of the President, he -immediately caused about 80 persona, who were believed to be disaffected, to be throwninto prison. 'Among the suspects was Greeibral Sully, who, finding that he hadlallen under the ban, con- trived to make good • his escape. The, General's wife, however, •vrho did not accompany herthus- band, was arrested. The =t3th of May, being the Feast of Corpus 'Christi, was a national holiday, and it was ceportediin order effectually to terrify the population General ,Hypolvte had commanded that a Gatling gun should• betaken into the gaol, andthat the 80 captives shouldbe summarily executed. The friends of the prisoners, among them being General Sully, met in Council, and revolved upon a bold stroke. Seizing their opportunity:while the President was attending ser- vice in the cathedral, they proceeded to the prisongorced open the eloorsrand set free the whale body of prisoners, to the number of-about 260. Then, by the express order of the President; there began, says a correspondent, a series of assassinations which probably is unequalled in the annals of civilisation, and in comparison with which the massaereofaint Bartholomew sinks into insignifi- cance.

div.head: DEATH OF TIIE,`CANADIAN PREMIER
div.p: DEATH OF TIIE,`CANADIAN PREMIER

BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCH. Sir .1-ohn Macdonald wh-, has been ill some time died painlessly at ',10.115 p.m. on Saturday. The deceased statesman was born in Scotland, in 1815. His father was a native of Sutherlandshire, and emi- grated to Canada, and took up his residence at Kingston, when his son was six years of age. The future Premier received his entire education at the Kingston Grammar School, and issaid to havetieen one of the best read and cultuired men in the IDominion, and a good classical scholar. Having. adopted the law as his profession, he was called, in :1E36, to the Bar of Upper Canada and 9 founded the legal firm of Maedocald and March ,of Toron- to, pra,ctisingifor eight years. Ire became a Q.C.,in 1846, but before thistime had commenced his political career, having been returned to Parliament in 1844, as a 'Conser- vative for'Kingston." He continued to represent Kingston until 1878, when he was elected for Victoria (British Columbia). He remained the representative of this con- stituency for four years, being elected in 1882 for Carle- ton (Ontario). In 1887 he was again returned for Kingston, which he -represented until his death. He returned to power in October, 1878, on the fall of the Mackenzie /Reform. Government, and took the posts of Minister of the Interior and Premier of the Dominion, which he heldnmtil the general election of March last. The Ministry were challenged on the question of com- mercial union with the 'United States, and were seked to *test the opinion of the country. Sir John Macdonald I accepted thischallengeeand was returned to power by a I considerable majority. His personal popularity in the Dominion was very greatiand his position in this respect was considered to be se much akin to that occupied by Ir. Gladstone in thistountry that he received the title of" Grand Old •Man of Canada." The "Canadian Dizzy" lams, however, a more acceptable title, the deceased ' st atesman being a greatadmirer of the late Lord Beacons- fie to whom he bore a certain facial resemblance. In 1865 the University of Oxford conferred on him the honor- er: 7 degree of D.C.L. Hewes made a Privy Councillor of Great Britain in 1872, and was sworn in in 1879. He wa a created K.C:B. in 1867, and was knighted in 1884. He was also a Knight of the Grand Cross of the Spanish Order of Isabella the Catholic. He was married' twice, the second time in 2.867. FUNEKAL ARRANGEMENTS.

KINGSTON, THURfIRAY.—The late Premier's remains „arrived here last night, and .amidst universal signs of ,mourning were removed to the City Hall. All public buildings and many private houses are draped in black, ,and there can be no dsubt that the obsequies this after- •rkocn will be the most imposing ever witnessed in Canada.

Gaming THE action for slander in the great. and Ch card case has ended, as it could eating . only end, if the jury were to have- any rogard for evidence, and that is in a verdict. for the defendants. It would have been a pity for all the parties concerned if there had been any: doubt as to. the issue, for that would have meant a .disagreement of the jury, and, in all likelihoodie new trial. We may be quite sure, if there had ' been any doubt amongst those who watched the - play of Sir WILLIAM GORDON GUMMING at Tranbp r Croft, that they would have given him the benefit. of that doubt, and the public would have heard ,nothing whatever of the matter. But if some of those who took part in the game wore to believe their own eyes, the acts of cheating were not • isolated :. they were systematic and unmistakable. The verdict of the jury, after a long and careful trial of the ease, is that the five defendants were justified in stating they saw the 'plaintiff cheat at _ cards ; and Sir WILLIAM GG.RDON-CUMMING ,110 W .standabefore the world with a mark which is • almost as the mark of Cain upon his brow. ludeed, when the Sear of disclosure-was upon him, he him-- self suggested that he might put an end to his life; and it was evidently this., which the Lord Chief Justice had in his mind when in summing up he, said.:—"They would ask themselves could a man.: of honour, who was certain in his own mind that, he was. innocent, under,. any circumstances write; himself down a cheat? Would he nal-ether have' put a pistol tohis head and shot himself.". SHAREB-- [' PEAR& expresses a similar thought in "Troilus and. 'Cressiela :"
Life every man holds dear ; but the brave man Holds honour far more precious-dear than life.

Sir WILLIAM was dishonoured from the moment he signed the document which he himself regarded aa conhassion of his gpilt ; and he is. to-day doubly- dishonoured in. that he has failed in the attempt to punish people in a court of. law who were the witnesses of truth. The charge which they brought against him was certainly e terrible one; but it is justified in law &sin °quit, because it is proved to be true in substance and in fact. If the law is to take its course—ani we do not see why it should not—the plaintiff should novz be placed in the dock as one who according to the testimony of unimpeachable witnesses has been guilty of misdemeanour br cheating at cards. Knaveaof all kinds are being sent to gaol every day for offences of a less serious character, and we do not, see why an exception should be made in favour of WltuAsit Gounorr- CUMMING because he happens ta be a knight as well as a knave.

It does not follow, of course,, that because the plaintiff in this case is found to be a great sinner, the rest of the party are necessarilY saints. They are all more or less tarred with one brush in that they were engaged in gaming at Tranby Croft; but, and this cannot be too fullY borne in mind, there is a wide gulf fixed between the gamester and the cheat. It was pleaded on behalf of the plaintiff, that he signed the compro- mising document because he wished to save the PRINCE of WALES from being mixed up with a scandal. But where was the scandal, if Sir IVILLIAO was innocent? It was the fact that there WaS a cheat at the gaming table that was likely to.give rise to a scandal. It is absurd to suppose any sane person would have signed away his' honour'

and thus shut himself off from the society of the PRINCE, when the only object was to save the PRINCE being talked about in connction with an ordinary game of baccarat. The person who so far lost his head would be ready for a lunatic asy- lum, and the people who took advantage of such Insanity would be deserving of the treadmill. But having said this much, it still remains to be remarked that the PRINCE of WALES is presented in a light which is not calculated to excite admira- tion for his habits and character. The Lord Chief Justice was good enough to say that he did not know that His Royal Highness did any particular harm if he enjoyed himself in the evening at a - game of baccarat. But for onselves we do see harm. It is not a good example to set to go to Doncaster and encourage horse racing and betting; and it is certainly a bad example to be party, the same evening, to setting up a gaming table at the house of a friend. It is known that Mr. WILSON Of Tranby Croft disapproved of baccarat ; but itis known, too, that the PRINCE or WALES desired a game, and that he provided the counters with Which the gam Q was played. His Royal Highness 18 usually regarded as a gentleman in the best sense of the term; but it is not the act of a gentleman to commence gamingin a house,contrary to the wishes of the host.- Apart, however, from this minor issue, gaining and batting are vices which are on the increase; and we have a right to look to those who are maintained in state and by the State to set such an example as will make it easier to do right and harder to do wrong. That this is not to be attaineta by playing baccarat is shown by the fall of Sir William GORDON-CUMMING—a fall of a friend, in the house of a friend, under such circum- stances as ought to cause the PRINCE to solemnly pledge himself never again to take part in a game of chance with money for the stake.

THE Government have introduced The Education their education measure, and, Bill, though it has some good features, it does not wholly satisfy any class—not even of their own supporters. What they are offering cannot strictly be called Free Education, because in the better class elementary schools, where the fee has exceeded threepence per week, there will still be something to pay. It is proposed that there shall be a special grant of 10s. per head upon the average attendance ; and this will mean freeing all schools where the fee is one of threepence per week O r less than that sum. But where the fee has been more than threepence, a small fee will'still have to be paid. For instance, as Sir W. HART- LYRE said in explaining the Government proposals, "a five-penny school would become a twopenny feed-school." "Twopenny feed" is suggestive as a rule of something for the body rather than the mind, and the odd phrase certainly tickled the fancy of the House on Monday even- ing. It will be seen that a plan of this kind Will be greatly to the advantage of schools with low fees ; while it will actually handicap some of the very best schools, where the average fee exceeds threepence per scholar. It is pleaded O n behalf of the proposal that it will apply to fully three-fourths of the scholars now attending .elementary schools; but, it is reasonable to ask, if education is to be free to three-fourths of the scholars, why not to the other fourth? Why make two bites at the cherry? These are ques- tions which are being asked of the Government, but no satisfactory answer is forthcoming. It seems to us that the object of the Government is to bolster up sectarian schools where the fees hap- pen to be low, and, by grants which in some cases will exceed the fees, set up an endowment fund which may be adroitly used for sectarian purposes. It is no secret that in some denominational schools a portion of the Government grant is at present applied, by a little manceuvring, to denomina- tional ends. How will it be when at a school, say, of 1,000 scholars, an extra £5OO a year is placed in the hands of irresponsible managers? Is there any citizen who values probity in public affairs Who can regard the prospect without misgiving? The measure will pass, we trust, even with the imperfections on its head, for, when, in the ordinary course of things, the Liberals come into power, this Fancy Education Bill, like the Fancy Franchise Bill brought in by Mr. DISRAELI, will serve as a basis of reform. It will end in being stripped of its fancy features, and in our obtaining Free Education pure and simple, along with popular control. The latter is indis- pensable, for education, however free it may be. nominally,will really be paid for either by means of rates or taxes, or both. In so far as rates are at Present drawn upon by means of School Boards for the purposes of education, expenditure is safe- guarded by official audit, and by the snpervision of representatives appointed by the ratepayers. It must be the same, or pretty much the same, with the funds furnished from the national exchequer. "It is not good enough," as the phrase goes, to take Two Millions from taxes and hand it over to School Managers, saying—" Make a proper use of this; but there will be no audit; and no tePresentative control." As the bill stands, there is no provision whatever for supplying due repre- sentative control; and it is therefore utterly vicious in its lack of princ;ple. The Government know this just as well as the Opposition, but they seek not so much to free education as to offer a double bribe—a bribe in the first place to the electors, and a bribe in the second place to the existing bodies of school managers. So far as the electors are con- cerned, it would seem, from recent by-elections, that they are not to be tempted with something Which would certainly come from the Liberals, if it didn't come from the Tories; and as to school managers it remains to be seen whether they will be grateful for a change which will subject them to obtrlvation and criticism and leave them in a state of suspense _for, it may be, a considerable time. Then there tire some Tory members of the House of Commons who do not like the Bill, and who do not like the Government for bringing it in. Mr. HOWARTH protested against it, on Monday, in good set terms; and he was supported by Sir R. TEMPLE and Mr. BARTLEY. These gentlemen wish it to be Understood that they are not equal as yet to 44 jumping Jim Crow." But they will of course Jump —after another protest or two. Meantime the Government have committed themselves; they have entered the wood, but they are not yet out of it.

div.head: "TuUCII AND GO."
div.p: "TuUCII AND GO."
"Inquirer."—Baccarat is a French game of cards; a game of chance—not of skill. The word is pro- nounced " bac-ca-ra," with the accent on the first syllable.
On Monday, Sir 'William Gordon-Cumming was " ruined " by the verdict in the baccarat case. On Tuesday he got married: "Tab/eau."

On page 2, there will be found an article by Mr. NV. Whitha: a on the " Drink Question," itl which he gives a bit of biography of a most interesting kind. It will be followed by a second paper in which our correspondent gives his views on High Licence.

A local contemporary gives, week by week, what is called a list of the attendances o local members in Parliament. This year, a cipher has invariably been found opposite the name of Sir G-ilbtrt Greenall. Does this mean that the member for Warrington has ceased to attend to his duties? Or is it one way of suggesting that he is a cipher in politics ? -

It would seem as if the " Howley • death-trap" is to be closed at last. it is estimated that a score of lives have been lost through the brook boing open and accessible to children. The maxim of the law is that wherever there is a wrong there is a remedy ; but who can point out the remedy to the parents who have lost their little ones ? The latest victim was a little boy—three years of age.

Of the vagaries of the art world there is no end. " The Angelus," a painting by Millet, the French artist, has just been purchased by a Londoner for £4,500. When the artist was living he received so little for his works that he could scarcely keep the wolf from the door ; and he painted this par- ticular picture for something less than £IOIJ. The producer starves, while the dealer waxes fat. " Tis a mad world, my masters."

The Tories seem to have come to the conclusion that the Liberal Unionist is played out. Hence the dispute at Barrow as to whether a Tory must take the field rather than a Liberal Unionist. Alas, for the "National party" which was to arise out of the fusion of the two—it is as far off as ever.

_ it is the same locally; the Liberal Unionist is thrown aside as a sucked orange. Indeed, there are Tories who even venture to speak of him with disrespect. In the Whitecross Ward election, in Warrington, Tory canvassers have actually urged Liberals not to vote for the Liberal candidate because he had been understood to be a Liberal Unionist! As if the fact that they were opposing him was not the best testimony to his character as a Liberal! •

The proper designation of Mr. Plumpton how- ever is that of Radical. He is in favour of Home Rule all round, manhood suffrage, and the aboli- tion of the House of Lords. In his speech to the electors, on Monday night, he made a capital im- pression, discussing local and referring to national topics in a way which showed that he has given thought to these matters, and that he has a mind of his own. The electors of the ward know him, and believe in him; and, despite the misrepresen- tation to which he has been subject, he will be returned, on Monday, by a large majority.

Both candidates, by-the-by, are opposed to any person directly interested in the drink trade having a seat upon the Watch Committee. When Mr. Alfred Woods answered a question to this effect, at the meeting on Wednesday night, Coun- cillor Bolton looked unutterable things; and shortly afterwards left the platform and left the the meeting. An observer summed up the situa- tion by saying " Hallo ! Bolton's bolted." Mr( Woods, it should be added, does not approve or Local Option, while Mr. Plumpton, is in favour of that policy.

The Borough Surveyor has issued a circular to all Warrington manufacturers calling atter Lion to clauses in the Public Health Acts Amendment Act,lB9o, as to penalties for turning refuse into the sewers. There is reason to believe certain firths in the town foul the sewers systematically. The stench is at times " something awful." It is to be hoped they will mend their ways, or, if they do not, that the Act will be enforced without fear it'd without favour.

The large attendance, on Sunday, at the funeral (1! the late Mr. Thomas Jolley amply testified to the sorrow for his untimely death. It can hardly be doubted that his willingness to serve led to his over-taxing himself as a cricketer and football player. Exercise up to a certain point is stimulating and healthful ; when it becomes ex- haustive, it is depressing and harmful. As the young do not know when to cry "Hold—enough !" their elders should keep a watchful eye and do it for them.

Two Irish labourers were brought before the Warrington magistrates, on Monday, for commit- ting a breach of the peace by trying to knock each other to pieces. D.S. Monaghan who gave evidence, said "there was blood flying about ;" but the men protested that they " were only in sport." The magistrates seemed to think the -men ought to have another opportunity of enjoying themselves, for they were discharged on paying costs. Perhaps it doesn't much matter so long as the blood is their own which is sent" flying about."

It is an ancient but barbarous joke to remove the chair when a person is in the act of sitting down. It has been often repeated; and repeated once too often. At the Liverpool County Court,on Monday, Mr. E. C. Staidley was called upon to pay £46 17s. 6d. for indulging in the time-honoured trick. It produced a spinal injury to the victim, Mr. E. 0. Windle ; and after hearing the evidence, the jury returned a verdict for the full amount claimed. There might be room to hope that the joke has been played for the last time; but—ah, these "buts "—thb fools are a prolific race.

The failure of the Warrington magistrates to convict in the case of Sunday. trading, the other week, has resulted in a large increase in the ob- jectionable practice. After what was said from the Bench, the Chief Constable feels that his hands are tied; and, if the butcher is allowed to do as he pleases, the grocer, the baker, and the candlestick-maker will conclude that they, too, hate an equal right to break the law. And where is the matter to end? Is the day of rest to be abolished? Or are we, in the language of the song, to act as if the devil was dead, and all just do as we like?

St. Helens County Court Judge is happily relieved of what might have proved a very knotty case for him. The issue as laid before him, on Wednesday, was whether a colliery proprietor could lawfully take a miner from coal getting, and put him on other and less remunerative work. Before the case was gone into, however, an arrangement was entered upon to refer the matter to the Mayor of St. Helens, or some other mutually acceptable person, the object being not so much to settle the point of law as to provide a working basis for the future. And why not ? Arbitration can accom- plish this, if anything can.

Mr. Justice Mathews gave an important decision on Saturday, in the case of the Hull and Holder- ness Conservative Permanent Building Society. It seems that the Secretary committed defalca- tionsito the extent of £14,000, and then committed suicide. A number of depositors by way of a test case sought to make the directors responsible, on the ground that the Secretary acted as their agent and that he continued to invite deposits after the borrowing powers of the Society were exhausted. The Judge held that the directors were personally liable, and gave a verdict for the plaintiffs with costs. This is a hard case for the directors against whom there is no imputation of fraud; but it will have the effect of causing other Boards to look more closely after secretaries, and thus be the means of safeguarding t!ke moneys of other share- holders and depositors.

div.head: ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN.
div.p: ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN.

On Monday evening a labourer named Alexander Ilannans was walking on the edge of the Bridgewater Lock which is in course of construction in the River, when his foot slipped and he fell. His fall was fortu- nately broken by alighting on a beam, or it is probable he would have been killed. He sustained a fractured leg, and was at once taken to Castle Rock, where Mr. Mission- ary Shaw put the injured limb in splints and eased the poor fellow's pain. He was afterwards conveyed to Latchford Hospital. PREMIER SAFETIES, Cash Or Hire.—GARLAND, Warrington. —Advt.

During the relief business at Runcorn Board of Gum', dians last week, Mr. E. Alron brought before the atten- tion of the Board a case of great interest to the working population of the district. Edward Roberts of Weston, died a short time ago, and at his death his widow became entitled to £l5 from the Prudential Insurance Company, but the age put upon the coffin did not agree with the age in the Company's books, and only £8 15s. was handed over to the widow. Mr. Aaron informed the Board that this man had paid premiums for no less a time than forty years, and if the Company had wished might easily have ascertained his accurate age. If he had lived another 40 years they would still have received his money. The woman would soon require relief from the Union and he thought the Board should take it up.— The Chairman said they could not do so until the woman applied for relief.—Mr. T. Lea said if she could prove that the correct age had been given she would get the money.—Mr. Ward (relieving officer) said in a similar case in London the plaintiff was given lull amountclaimed and costs.

NOT BACCARAT THIS TI24R.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr Handley and Dr. Steele, Joseph Bushell, John Lamb, Thos Flannigan, John Flannigan. Thos. Findlay, Christopher Connell, T. Connell, and T. Robinson, youths, pleaded guilty to having on Sunday, the 31st May, on the Fair Ground, played with cards for a means of gaming.—P.C. Crowder and P.C. Jones gave evidence.—Supt. Large said gambling by cards and tossing was greatly on the increase, and the complaints were numerous on each Sunday. He was obliged to put three or four constables in plain clothes every Sunday, and ho wished their wor- ships to help them to stamp the evil out.—Mr. Handley: Are these youths working during the week.—The Supt. replied that a number of them loitered about the railway station, parcel carrying.— Mr. Handley said there were plenty of Sunday schools for them to go to.—The Supt.: Oh yes, sir.—Bushell, Thomas Flannigan, and Robinson were each fined is. and costs as. 6d. and the remainder 6d. and costs Bs. 6d. each.—Two boatmen named Samuel Lighthall, and Edward Bond, were each ordered to pay 4s. 6d. costs for playing pitch aud toss on the Stone Hills on the 12th May.
SUCCESS OF A RUNCORN YOUTH.

We are please to announce that in connection with the annual Cadet Competition of the National Division of the Sons of Temperance of Great Britain and Ireland, held at Sheffield,in Whit week last ; which comp3tition,embraces various sections, and classes, and is open to all juvenile members of the order in the United Kingdom ; the adjudicators in class 111 sections, writing, and drawing, open to all juvenile members above eleven and under fourteen years of age, awarded the first prize to Master John D. Bisbrown, son of Mr. Daniel Bisbrown, of Greenway-road, Runcorn, for the best penmanship,in copying a piece of composition. subject, strong drink. Master Bisbrown also secured the second prize, for the best drawing to scale, half inch to foot, of outline of front elevation of a two-storied house, 40 feet frontage, 22 feet from ground to eaves, door in centre, two bay windows on ground floor, and three windows above, all finished in ink. We understand this is the first effort of our young friend, in connection with the competitions. We therefore congratulate him on his success. It may be of interest to know that Master Bisbrown is a scholar attending the Brunswick Wesleyan Day School, and no little credit is due to Mr.B. Crosby, the schoolmaster, for the youth's success. CRICKET': CRUSHING DEFEAT OF LANCASHIRE. The play in the match Lancashire v. Middlesex was resumed yesterday at Lords, and Lancashire was heavily beaten by the home team. The scores were—Middlesex First innings, 96; second, 166. Lancashire : First innings, 63; second, 67. Mr. S. M. Crosfie.ld, the Warrington captain, played in the Lancashire eleven. AN INCIDENT OF THE RACES. At the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday, before Mr. A. C. McCorquodale, a man named John Jones, of no fixed residence, was brought up in custody charged with being found on the premises of Mr. James Ellison, license of the Griffin Hotel, Hotel, on on the previous night, with intent to commit a felony. From the evidence adduced, it appeared that Mrs. Ellison observed a man go up the stairs about 9.30 en Friday night, and so informed her husband. Mr. Ellison went upstairs and found the. prisoner in the servant's bedroom, crouching down, by the aide of the bed. Mr. Ellison seized him and threw him on the floor, where he held him until the arrival of P.C. Milner, of West Leigh, into whose custody he was given. When searched there was found on the prisoner a small pick lock for opening drawers, a wedge, a piece of candle, and sundry other articles. Prisoner was remanded to Newton Petty Sessions to-day (Saturday.) He was photo- graphed by Mr. Unsworth for the police, as it was supposed he was an old offender. THE FAILURE OF A RAINHILL TRADER. On Tuesday, at the Wrexham Bankruptcy Court, Robert Jackson, formerly of Rainhill, near Prescot, but now residing at Llanymynech, near Gswestry, and carrying on business as a timber merchant, again came up for his public examination. The official receiver (Mr. Ll. Hugh Jones) questioned him respecting his interest under his late father's will. He said he was entitled to a seventh share. The net probate only amounted .to £l9l 16s. 10d. His father had some house property in St. Helens a chain and bolt manufactory, and a timber yard and saw mill. Both businesses were still being carried on by his brother Peter Jackson, who was a licensed victualler. There was a mortgage on the properties, but he did not know the amount. His wife I,ad no income of her own. He lost £7O by be- coming guarantor for two persons. He had no secur- ity for this money.—Mr. R. W. Glaseodine, who ap- peared for Mr. Mearns, solicitor, Liverpool, cross- examined the debtor as to statements he was alleged to have made to Mr. Mearns. He said he had been in the habit of betting, but he never bet more than £5 at a time. Ile had not kept any account of his betting transactions. He only betted when he went to race meetings.—The Official Receiver pointed out that the debtor had been ordered by the Court to furnish a cash account, a profit and less account, and a trading account, for the three years preced- ing the date of his bankruptcy. He (the official re- ceiver) had only received one of these accounts, and he submitted that even this account did not at all ' comply with the terms of the order.—The registrar said he would make a fresh order on the bankrupt to furnish these accounts.—The further examination was then adjourned to the next court.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL ' BOARD,
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL ' BOARD,

The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday under the presidency of Mr. B. Brown. Present, Dr. O'Keeffe. Messrs. S. Sadler, J. Houghton, J. Taylor, F. Heyes, J. Tilley, G. I. Neil, H. S. Timmis, Oppenheim (c k) Hoyle (accountant), Carr (en- gineer), Sinclair (surveyor). The Chairman said before going on with the regular business of the meeting they ought to recognise the death of their caretaker Mr. George Hackney. He had served the Board faithfully and well and although it was in a humble capleity,he was none the less deserving of their respect.—The Clerk was instructed to convey a vote of condolence to the bereaved widow.

GAS AND WATER-PROFIT AND LOSS. The Gas and Water Committee reported that accounts amounting to £776 15s. on gas account and £3Ol 9s. sd. lon water account were examined and passed for pay- ment. Mr. E. Carey, secretary, to the United Alkali Company had discussed the question of water charges with the Committee and Mr. Carey agreed with the proposals of the Committee and the Clerk was instructed to prepare an agreement with the Company with respect thereto. The gas was tested on the 21st and 29th May, when the Illuminating power a as respectively 1926. and 1932. sperm candles, free from sulphuretted hydrogen. Samples of the water from Stocks well and Netherley had been submitted to Mr. Campbell Brown for analysis, and he reported both to be of excellent quality—clear and colourless without deposit.—The }..ngineer reported that about midnight. on the 16th inst., the 12-inch main in Cromwell-st. burst. The metal of the pipe was found to be very much decomp?sed, necessitating the renewal 'of four lengths. The mains throughout the whole of this district are in a rotten state, due to the action of the slag and cinders in which they are laid. The proposed waste water meter for this district would shortly be fixed, which would enable any leakage to be much more readily detected. 'Fhe mean rainfall for the month had been 2.07 inches. Tlid Water in stock on May 27th was 7,451,894 gallons. 'Du? wages required during the next five weeks for gas and water works, £lO6 per week. The profit and loss accounts were submitted and approved and showed a I,4ss of £292 6s. 6d. on gas account and profit of £1,747 us. 7d. on water accaunt.—Mr. Brown moved the adoption of the minutes, and referring to the loss on the gas works, said during the year they had been working on a lower priced coal, and although they had not got so many cubic feet of gas from the ton of coal used as in the previous, year they had got a larger quantity of residuals. This result had been helped forward by the Dinsmore process; 25 or 30 per cent, of their retorts being worked on that principle. The increased price of the residuals had been considerable and they had received something like £BOO or £9OO more for coke than last year, and about £2OO more for tar ; so that they thought it was pos- sible to pursue this policy of using inferior coal in conjunction with the Dinsmore process and get more coke, tar, and sulphate of ammonia. Of course , they had to use more coal. During the year they ' had had a large amount of special expenditure and there was a great loss consequent on the flood. Under all the circumstanees the balance was very good. If they had charged the same price for gas as was charged in a neighbeuring town, they might have been able to- show a profit of about £4,000. As to the water account, the cost of pumping had been greatly increased during the year, through the increased price of fuel. They had paid something like £BOO more for fuel than was paid last year. They had also suffered very much from leakage but they hoped to overcome that before long. Under all the circumstances the Board would agree that the results were very favourable.—Mr. Wright seconded the motion. The minutes were passed.

div.head: THR HEALTH COMMITTEE. HIGFLEtTH RATH
div.p: THR HEALTH COMMITTEE. HIGFLEtTH RATH

The Health Committee instructed the Clerk to reply to Mr. J: G. Rhodes, repudiating any lianility for the re- moval of bricks by night soil men. The Medical Officer reported that during May there were 102 births and 81 deaths ; being at the respective rges of 3948 and 31.35. Them were 23 deaths amongst children under one year and T between one and five years. Zymotic diseases caused 3 deaths. Notifications of infectious disease had been received as follows :—Erysipelas 2, scarlatina 1, membraneous croup 1. The higk death rate was doubt- less due to the epidemic of influenza and to the rapid change of temperature experienced during the month. 'There were four inmates in the Accident Hospital and three in the Fever Hospital. The Nuisance Inspector was instructed to take proceedings for the removal of certain nuisances. The receipts for the month from the market were £33 18s.4d.,being a decrease of £l5 153.7 d. as compared with May, 18901. caused by the receipts from the Fair Ground and river shore having fallen from £29 3s. 11d., last year, to £l5 Us. 4d. this year, and in con- sequence of the abolition of hawkers' toll.—Mr. Wright moved the adoption of the minutes. Mr. Timmis se- conded.—Carried.

div.head: FINANCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: FINANCE COMMITTEE.

The Finance Committee recommeaded upon their ap- plications that the salaries of the following officials in the accountant's department be increased as follows :—Chas. Whitfield,collector, from £llO to £l2O per annum, Thos. H. Wilson, chief Clerk, from £lOO to £l2O and Isaac- Sankey assistant collector from £75 to £9O. Recom- mended that permission be given to the Lancashire County Council to attach a telephone wire to the Town Hall for the purpose of connecting the Widnes. and Warrington Police Divisions, and that the Clerk be authorised to sign the forth of consent subbmitted. The accountant reported that under sanctions of the Local. Government Board dated respectively sth July, 1883, 27th August, 1886, 16th July, 1888, and 27th February, 1889, the Local Board were authorised to borrow £20,752 for works of street improvement, of that sum £16,800 had been borrowed, of which £9,201) had been paid off by the amoants received from property owners. He therefore suggested that application should be made to the Local Government Bnard to have such sanctions cancelled to the extent of the payments actually made and to the amount which, had never been borrowed. Recommended that application be made accordingly. Accounts amounting to £6,182 15s. 9d. were recommended for payment IMr. Houghton moved and Mr. Tilley seconded the pass- ' ing of the minutes.—Mr. Heyes moved that the minute relating to intreases of salary be struck out. In his opinion it was a farce, because all the officials of the Board would go out of office in a few months, and the whole staff would have to be reorganised. This recom-. mendation appeared tobe an attempt to fetter the action of the Corporation.—Mr. Wright said the staff had been under paid for a long time, but he could not say he agreed with the manner in which the advances were given, the increases were not proportionate.—Mr. Heyes moved and Mr. Sadler seconded an amendmentthat the recommendation be referred back to the Committee and this was carried by five votes to three.
THE PROPOSED BRIMS. ACROSS THE MERSEY.

The General Purposes Committee reported that the de- putatlon from the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners Consisting of Messrs. S. Taylor (chairman), F. Wiswall, with the Committee and F. A. Lake (law clerk), attended the meeting and discussed the question of a proposed bridge and the further consideration of the matter was deferred.—ln reply to Mr. Sadler the Chairman said the minute showed all that had been done. He did not see what they could do ; they had not a million of money to spend.

div.head: HOSPITAL MANAGEMENT.
div.p: THE HOSPITAL MANAGEMENT.

Mr. Wright said he had expected the gentlemen who bad made complaints with respect to the adminis- tration of the Hospital. If these gentlemen would in- vestigate the establishment for themselves, they would find that no extravagance was carried on, Remarks had been made about the high gas bill at the Accident Hospital but a large number of bad cases accounted for this. As to the gardening a large quantity of vegetable and flower seeds had been sown, and they hoped to have a good crop of vegetables, and the Board would be able to recoup themselves. Either the Committee must have the institutions efficient or inefficient, and they courted the fullest scrutiny and investigation. Mr. Mid- wood who had been prominent in his complaints had only once entered his name in the visitors book, and if gentlemen would not visit the hospital, they ought not to make remarks reflecting on the committee.—Mr. Tay- lor : I am afraid that the members would not have the courage to go.—Mr. Wright, alluding to the wages of two men at the Fever Hospital—£llo--explained that formerly a man was borrcwed from the Highway Com- mittee, and the men were fully employed in putting the place in a proper state of efficiency, so that the Board could cope with an epidemic. He moved that a corn-' mittee cqnsisting of members other than the Health Committe,investigate and examine the work done at the Hospital, and ascertain whether they had been justified in doing that work.—Dr. O'Keeffe said in his capacity as a medical man, he had to visit both hos- pitals while these works had been going on, and he did not see that there was any .unnecessary expenditure being carried on.—Mr. Hayes said Mr. Cook and Mr. Midwood were the only two who protested, and if Mr. Wrlght would move that those gentlemen form the committee he would second it.—Mr. Wright : I move that.—Mr. Hayes: I second.—Mr. Taylor moved that Mr. Sadler's name be added to the committee.—The Chairman suggested that the mitter might be investi- gated at the general inspection.—Mr. Sadler: If you leave it o the annual inspection you would not be able to discover how much beer had been drunk the previous month.—The Clerk decided that Mr. Wright's motion could not be dealt with until due notice had been given and the discussion then ceased.

div.head: WIDNES DIVISION LIBERAL ASSOCIATION. sPEECH BY MR. 11. WADE DEACON.
div.p: WIDNES DIVISION LIBERAL ASSOCIATION. sPEECH BY MR. 11. WADE DEACON.

The annual public meeting for the purpose of appointing the Widnes District Council and elect- ing 26 representatives to the Divisional Executive Committee was held in Lacey-st. Schoolroom, on Thursday evening. Mr. E. Carey presided and there were present Mr. H. Wade Deacon, 3.P., Liberal candidate for the division, Rev. Dean Finegan, Rev. Father Clarke, Major Wareing, Messrs. T. Snape, C.C. F. H. Pankhurst, S. Owens, F. Hartland, Showan, H. Johnson, F. Lawrenson, 11, B. Shores (secretary), &c. The room was filled with an enthusias- tic audience. After the various represe:itatives had been chosen and elected Mr. Deacon delivered an address. Referring to his opponent he said they were not fighting against any particular man, they were fighting for prin- ciples in which they believed and which would be vic- tcrious at the first opportunity. If they were not vic- torious in Widnes they would be victorious in the coun- try and having such a good cause they had no need to abuse their opponent; and he hoped they should pre- serve an excellent temper all through. In January Mr. Moss said Home Rule would be no message of peace to Ireland and that thousand of Englishmen were wavering on the subject. Since that speech there had been 12 elections in Great Britain. These twelve con- stituencies had returned nine Tories or Unionists and three Liberals; but now they were represented by six Liberals and six Tories. (Applause.) These results did not show that thousands of Englishmen were wavering; it looked as if Englishmen were still prepared to grant the demand for Home Rule. (Applause.) Since the General Election in 1886, 91 elections had taken place, in constituencies which had been represented by 621 opponents and 29 supporters of Home Rule—a majority of more than two to one against Home Rule. The , result of the elections showed 46 supporters and 45 opponents of Home Rule, or a majority of one in favour of Home Rule. (Applause.) These were very clear indeed and could anyone doubt that if it got the chance Widnes would follow the lead of other places. (Ap- plause.) He had great hopes that they would be suc- cessful, but it did not do to rely upon hope; it was necessary to have an active council, who would work and collect the voters together. (Hear, hear.) Alluding to the Irish question he said the soliition must satisfy the reasonable requirements of the two nations. Of course there was a body of men in Ireland who made unreasonable demands but he did not believe that the majority of the Irish people would support them. Speaking of education, Mr. Deacon said, as he had been on the School Board for twelve years his general line of action with regard to education sir as well known in Widnes. (Applause.) The population was increasing at a rapid rate, and not only had we to face the difficulties which were raised by that increase, but also the competition which came from other countries which were very much ahead of England in educational matters. It seemed to him, therefore, abso- lutely necessary that we should train the young people to use to the utmost capacity the abilities which God had given them. It would be impossible to make a child of poor capacity equal to a child which had been richly •en- dowed with brains, but it was possible so to educate and train children that the proportion of them which became

drunkards and brutes in future should be an ever dimin- ishing quantity. (Applause.) He welcomed free Edu- cation however it should come: because he knew from his experience on the District Education Coinmittee of the School Board that Free Education would prove a, boon to a great many poor people. (Hear, hear.) It would take all the force out of the complaint which one heard frequently "I cannot send the child to school be- cause I have no school pence." In his opinion these were not the people to whom Free Education would prove the greatest blessing. They did not send their children regularly when the fees were paid under present arrangements. He did not believe that Free Education would effect the average attendance of public element- ary schools. The paople who used that complaint did not use the correct one. The real reason for the irregularity of children might be summed up in the word " Drink. " The abolition of school pence would not abolish this curse, but Free Education must be welcomed by Liberals as a full admission of the .fact that the State is responsible for see- ing that every child born into the land should receive a measure of elementary education. (Applause.) But this was not sufficient; he must have more than that. It would be necessary for-the State to take sone action in regard to children who had recently left school. We ought to have a national system of secondary or intermediate schools. There-must be some connection between them and the elementary schools, by means of- free scholar- ships or some other means by which the clever chil- dren of poor, parents coald pass from the elementary schools into the higher schools,and on to the Universities, so that they should be trained to be of the greatest use to themselves and to their country. (Applause.) The whole thing- must be free. (Applause.) Alluding to the taxation of land, he said land escaped local rates in a most unjiist and unfair manner, and ought to he made to bear its fair share of rates and taxes. (Applause.) In conclusion Mr. Deacon said he should have other op- portunities of expressing his views., He hoped they would vote for him and induce others to do so. (Ap- plause.)*--Mr. Carey had to leave-to.cateh his train, and Major Wareing took the chair, and proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Deacon for his address.—Dr. O'Keeffe se- conded the motion, which was carried with much enthu- siasms—ln replying, Mr. Deacon. said he had overlookei the- temperance question, .whiclL was of the greatest im- portance to the country. He had for a long time con- sidered that control of the licensing laws ought to be vested somehow in the ratepayers. (Applause.)—A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the proceedings.

div.head: PRESCOI BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOI BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board o Guardians was held on Thursday week at Whiston Workhouse when there were present Mr. J. Birchall (chairman), Rev. D. Finegan, Revs. S. A. K. Sylvester and C. NV. Wooll, Messrs. Marsh, Graves, Johnson, Lowe, Davies, Peover, Daine, Whalley, E. Birchall, Mercer, Griffiths, W. B. Lonizton, Buckley, J. Ellison, Joseph Birchall, J. Ramon, Syder, P. Longton, Hulme, Borrows, Kenwright, and A. F. Mann, (acting-clerk). RELIEF.—The Workhouse master reported that the number of inmates this week was 463, last week 555, and corresponding week last year 479. During the first ten weeks of the present quarter 2,282 persons had been relieved against 3,102 in the corresponding period last vear, at a cost of £261 2s. id., against £263 1.95. 10d. last year. THE RESIGNATION OF Mn. LF.ATITERBARROW. A letter was read from the Local Government Board intimating that they had received and accepted the resignation of Mr. John Leatherbarrow. Dean ; Finegan moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Leather- barrow for his services to the Board remarking that he had always been one of its most efficient members. He also coupled the name of Mr. Win. Tyrer with the vote of thanks.—Major Waring seconded.—The resolution was carried, and it was decided to take the necessary steps for securing the election of Guardians for the townships of Winston and Prescot. THE CLEEKsilip.—The Local Government Board wrote acknowledging receipt of the communication informing them that Mr. Mann had been appointed acting clerk to the Guardians during the vaeuncy caused by the death of Mr. Hartley. The Board iiegretted to learn of Mr. Flartley's death,and asked to, be favoured with particu- lars of the appointment of a successor when duly made. —The Rev. Dean Finegan said he had been asked a ques- tion since he came into the Kim by Mr. Mercer as to whether Mr. Danlay had his authority or the authority of Major Waring for stating that they had sent him to canvass for his support before Mr. Hartley's funeral. He, on behalf of himself and Major Waring, could say that Mr. Danhy had no such authority. TEE LATE CLERK.—A letter was read from Mrs. S. Hartley, acknowledging the receipt of a letter of condo- lence and sympathy en the death of her husband, and thanking them for their kind expressions. APPOINTMENT OF A NEW CLERK.-1 he Board then pro- ceeded to deal with the applications of the four selected candidates for vacant clerkship to the Guar- dians. The four candidates were Mr. G. H. Danbv (Wid- nes), Mr. J. B. Goulburn (Bolton), Mr. H. Y. H. Lan- caster (Barton Regis, near Bristol). and Mr. A. F. Mann (Prescot),the latter being the present acting clerk to the Board. The qualifications and testimonials of each can- didate were discussed and the candidates were called into the room. The voting of the Guardians took place by ballot and the result was as follows : Mr. Mann 21 votes, Mr. Lancaster 2, and Mr. Danby and Mr. Goulburn one each. Mr. Mann was thereupon declared elected, and on being again called into the room and informed of the fact Mr. Mann expressed his sincere thanks for the honour they had done him and said he should always endeavour to carry out his dt:ties to the entire satisfaction of the Board, and to the best interest of that important and growing union. A resolution appointing Mr. Mann super- intendent registrar of Prescot district waS carried Unaniin- ousts,.
This was the principal busines3. RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. James namiley Atee!.

AN OFFENDING LODGING-HORSE.—Ann Farrell, Vicar- St., lodging-house keeper, was summoned by Mr. James Percival, Inspector of Nuisances' for uot keeping her house free from filth on the 3rd June. Mr. Lake pro- secuted on behalf of the Board of Commissioners, and the defendant was fined 10s., and costs Bs. 6d. DRUNKENNESS.—For this offence a fine of 2s. 6d. and costs was imposed upon Mary Murphy, Edward Oulton, and Henry Baker; and a fine of ss. and costs was im- posed upon Catherine Craig and William Smith. rhilt DANGER OF SLEEPY DRIVERS.—JOSeph Taylor, of Warrington, was summoned for being asleep while in charge of two horses and a brewer's wagon in Halton - road, on the night of the 3rd inst.—The defendant said he had had very long hours for many weeks past.—Mr. Handley: You will have to do same as the London 'bus- men and strike.—Superintendent Large said it was very dangerous; he had many near escapes coming home from the country at night.—Mr. Handley: And it is very singular they are always brewers' drays.—Superinten- dent Large: It is the beer that sends them off, sir.—A fine of 10s., and costs 10s. 6d. was imposed. THE STONE-THROWING NUISANCE. Joseph Neild, Edward Melia, Thomas Connolly, Joseph Rawson, Thos. Garritty, youths, were charged with having on the 4th June, wantonly thrown stones in Station-road, to the danger of passengers in the street.—Neild and Rawson pleaded guilty atti the rest not guilty.—P.C. Jones gave evidence.—Supenntendent Large said not many days be- fore Mr. Scott, the goods manager, nearly had his eye knocked out by a stone and a large quantity of goods had recently been smashed by this practice. Connolly was , dismissed and the remainder were each fined 6.1., and costs Bs. 6;l.—The Chairman warned that future offenders would receive severe punishment. A NAMELESS CART.—For not having his name printed on his cart, Frederick Chell, of Halton, was fined 2s. 6d. and costs Bs. 641. A VAGRANT.—John Young was sentenced to seven days' hard labour for begging in Sewell-street, on Sunday. The prisoner had called at the house where P.C. 159 lodged and asked for alms.
----.0.---. WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS.
THUIZSDAY.—iIefOre Mr. H. Wade Deacon and Mr.

_ Stapleton Bretherton. Datrxx.—John Bryan and Thomas Makin were each fined ss. and costs for this offence. AssauLT.—Edwin Clay, of Oxford-st., was bound over to keep the peace for assaulting a woman named Mary Moores. UNJUST Schass.—James Riley, coal dealer, Midwood- st., charged with haying in his possession an unjust weight 281b5., which was 11b. 20z., 9 drachms against the purchaser.—The defendant said he did not use the weight for businesss purposes ; but he was fined 10s.and costs, or 14 days in default. LIGHT Palin, bread baker, Ann-st. West, was summoned for selling bread otherwise than by weight, and also not carryityr scales in his cart to weigh bread. Inspector Kilpatrick"proved buying a 41b. loaf at the defendant's shop. He found that it was over 3oz. light, and next morning it was over soz. light. The de- fendant was fined 10s. and costs, on the second charge; the first charge was dismissed.

A RIOT IN MARSH-ST.—Margaret Forbes, Cromwell-st., Catherine Hynes, Michael Purcell, and Bridget Weir, of Marsh-st., were charged with doing wilful damage to certain window frames, and other property belonging to the Prescot Building Society, and to Ann Kinsella, of Marsh-street, to the amount of £l2.—Mr. J. W. Knowles prosecuted. On Whit Tuesday while Mrs. Kinsella was in bed, Hynes smashed open the door of the shop with a hatchet and the other defendants smashed the parlour window. On the following Thursday they took down the shutters and using them as rams, smashed the shop win- dows and Purcell broke the mantlepiece upstairs with a brick. The damage was £l2 and Mr. Knowles said it was a deliberate attempt to wreck the house. Fl3'nes and Weir old offenders were sent to gaol for a month; Forbes and Purcell were each fined Os. and costs, or 21 days' imprisonment.—Ann Kinsella, the complainant in the last cage, was charged with smashing five panes of glass in the window of the house of Catherine Forbes on the 31st May, and she was fined 10s. and costs or 21days imprisonment.
BRANDRETH'S SUGAR-COATED PILLS are a very safe medicine for children.—Advt.
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c. BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDRNT.

It is pleasant news that the Influenza Fiend has nearly been driven away from Runcorn. Unfor- tunately the disease is still rampant in. Widnes. The Navvies' and babourers' Union should have demonstrated at Runcorn, on Sunday last, with the view to forming a branch in the town, but the Trades Union who ought to have led the way did not turn up. They found more excuse for their energies in the business strike in LOfUlOll, an 4 the hundreds of Runcornians who nulled out were much disappointed, The demonstration is to come off to-morrow. Mr. Thomas Clarkson, cashier at Messrs. Golding, Davies, and Co.'s works, Widnes,. has juAt been appointed chief accountant of the United Alkali Company. Widnesians cannot complain that the plums of the great syndicate have not come their way. _ _ _

Tbe gas and water undertakings of the Widnes Local Board continue to prosper. Although the water is dispensed at an exceedingly low rate there is a profit OIL the year's working uf .£1,747. On gas there has been a loss of £292, but when it is con- sidered what extensions have taken place during the twelve months it is surprising that the adverse balance was not much larger. As Mr. Brown per- tinently remarked, did the Board charge as high a price for their gas as adjoining towns they could have shown the profit of £4,000. The ratepayers are fortunate in possessing two such admirable and well-managed undertakings. Os dit that a gentlemen of the legal profession, practising in the neighbourhood of Runcorn, was married a few days ago at a Welsh watering place, but the event was kept a close secret until after the happy event had taken place. The need of the Cottage Hospital was well shown the other day. On Wednesday week a Ship Canal worker had three fingers cut from one hand and had to be conveyed to Latchford. On the Thursday a sailor at the Docks got his leg entangled in a coil of rope, and the limb was broken in two places; he was conveyed to Liverpool Infirmary. On Monday last a labourer bad his leg broken on the Ship Canal Works. Hew much suffering might these man have been saved could they have been comfortably housed , at Ruecorn

3.1 r. Samuel Taylor's year of office as chairman of Runcorn Board of Commissioners has now termin- ated, and his successor will be appointed at the annual meeting. Although the year has not been ft very eventful one, yet it has been signalised by several good works, that will bear recapitulating, Waterloo Bridge has been widened and generally improved,after a weary waiting; the Aged Persons' Treat has been revived, and carried out with MD- cess ; the Technical Education Act has been adop- ted; and the Cottage Hospital is in a fatr way to establishment.

In all these undertakings Mr. Taylor has taken a most prominent part, and the deepest and. warm- est interest, and much credit is due to him for their accomplishment. He has filled thechair with dignity and good humour, and the business of the town has in consequence been conducted without any disagreements other than differences of opinion calmly expressed. In common with the rest of the ratepayers, I hope he may long live to serve the town in the various public positions he occupies and to again occupy the chair of our chief local , governing body. I hear a whisper that Mr. James Pritchard will be his successor.

div.head: SUICIDE ON RUNCORN BRIDGE.
div.p: SUICIDE ON RUNCORN BRIDGE.

Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, on Saturday held an inquest at Widnes, on the body of a man unknown, who was run over by an express goods train on Thursday afternoon,—lnspector Taylor (Edge Hill), was present on behalf of the railway company.—Richard Killener, 2, Dorfield-st., Crewe, engine driver, said on Thursday he was in charge of a goods train leaving Crewe at 2.25 for Liverpool. When crossing Runcorn Bridge he saw a man stand- ing on the line about 50 yards in front and when the train was about 20 yards away, the man crawled in front of the engine which passed over him. Wit- ness could not stop before reaching Ditton as he was travelling between two express trains,—Alfred Kilshaw, a boy, of James-st., Widnes, said he saw • the deceased on the bridge just before he was killed. He was leaning against the wall and appeared to have had some drink.—P.C. Worsfold said he met the deceased in Waterloo-road, on ThurNday morn- ing, and he asked the way to Runcorn Bridge. He said he had been knocking about Lancashire long enough and he would try Cheshire. Deceased ap- peared to be in a state of despondency and to talk as if half witted.—The jury returned a verdict that deceased committed suicide while in a state of tem- porary insanity.
HUSBANDS AND WIVES AT RUNCORN.

Before Mr. James Handley and Dr. Steele, at Runcorn Petty Sessions,on Monday, Daniel Fletcher, a painter, was summoned that he being able wholly to maintain hie wife, did wilfully neglect so to do and did desert ber,--.The woman said she was at present living with her daughter in Mill-st. The defendant went away on Sunday, the 30th March, ati,l had not yet returned, Ile did not leave her meat, money, or coal. lie was able to earn on an average 278. per week.—The defendant said it was through her drunken habits that he had to go. Ile had lived the life of a dog through her drunken habits. She had never been sober for six years. Would it be safe, he asked, to give a woman like that money to drink or throw away to the dogs. He had paid his daughter 53. per week for her.— Mrs. Fletcher said she knew nothing of this pay- ment until she had brought these proceeding.—The defendant said be would not live with his wife again, but was quite willing to maintain her.—The Bench made an order upon him to contribute Bs. per week towards his wi:e's support.—Peter Knight was apprehended under a warrant taken out by his wife Annie, for the sum of £1 ss.' arrears made under the Married Women's Maintenance Act.—Mr. Burton said this matter had been arranged ; the wife was satisfied.— The prisoner was discharged.—Richard Bushell, a flat.. man, was summoned by his wife Alice, that he being able wholly to maintain her and her family, had neg- lected to do so, and had deserted her.—She said she had been married 21 years, and lived at 25, Spring Cottages. Twelve weeks ago he left her, but he had frequently visited the house and smashed the crockery and furni- ture. She had never received any money from him since he loft. She did not wish for anything for herself, but for her three children ; she could keep herself by washing. —Defendant said his wife had broken four homes up in 21 years. He offered her 30s. a few days before Whit Monday, but she refused it.--The woman said she did not consider it enough for ten weeks.—The ddendant said he had been a teetotaller for 14 years, and had striven hard for his wife and family, but he could not get her to do what was right. She kept bad company, and visited St. Helens and Warrington, and she had even asked her brother to let her live at his house with another man. For three nights at Easter she was not at home, and when he asked where she had been she attempted to strike him with the poker.—Mr. Handley: You have undertaken the responsibility and you are bound to maintain her.— Mr. Johnson (assistant magistrates' clerk) : If you can prove that she has committed adultery then you are not liable.—The defendant: I am not going tc say that, but she keeps men in my house and turns them out at late hours at night. The neighbours could prove it.—Mr. Handley said he had no evidence, and an order would be made upon him to contribute 95. per week towards the support of his family. He had also to pay costs, 10s. ed.
