div.head: TRA-DES DEMONSTRATION.
div.p: THE TRA-DES DEMONSTRATION.

Mrs. Jones, of the Waggon and Horses, Buttermarket- st. applied to the Warrington magistrates yesterday for an extension of hours until 12 p.m. to-night on account of her being engaged to cater for 200 persons, who would take part in the trades procession to-day. The applica- tion was acceded to. A GANG OF JUVENILE RAILWAY THIEVES.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Wednesday, Henry Delooze, a youth, of 1, Lilford-st., John Thompson, aged 15, of 1, Knowles-st., William Alcock, aged 15, of 33, Winwick-road, Thos. Boardman, aged 15. of 44, Fennell- at., and Edward Ashbrook, aged 14, of 115, Orford-lane, were charged with stealing that morning, from a rail- way van in the Dallam siding, a quantity of saccharine, the property of the London and North-Western Railway Company. AU the lads pleaded guilty.—Railway Detec- tive Atkinson said in consequence of the complaints re- ceived of the pilfering of saccharine from the vans, he watched that morning about five o'clock and saw Delooze come and open a sack of saccharine lying in a van, and fill his pockets. He followed him and took him into cus- tody, and ascertained that the.other prisoners were con- cerned in the theft of about 30Ibs. of saccharine, com- mitted about half-past six the previous morning.—They admitted their guilt, and had distributed the saccharine amongst their companions in the robbery, who were em- ployed with them by the Warrington Wire Rope Com- pany. The Railway Company had lost about half a ton of this saccharine through boys filling their pockets with it.—Delooze was fined Bs. including costs, and the other prisoners ss. each, including costs.

div.head: CHARGE OF THEFT AGAINST A SERVANT.
div.p: CHARGE OF THEFT AGAINST A SERVANT.

At the Borough Police Court, yesterday, Agnes Lea, was charged with stealing a silver coin brooch, five towels, one pair of ladies' boots, one pinafore, one linen clothes bag, and other articles, value in all 305., the pro- perty of Thos. Pilkington, contractor, Bewsey-road. Chief-Constable Hunt said the prisoner and her aunt, Mary Sutton, had been living with a Mrs. Almond in Chester-st., Battarsby-lane. Mrs. Pilkington had adver- tised for a domestic servant.and the prisoner on Monday night went with her aunt and applied for the situation. They stated that she had not been in service before, and had no character ; but she had a good address, and Mrs. Pilkington engaged her. Mrs. Pilkington left the girl and two little children in the house, but on her return found the prisoner gone. Mrs.Pilkington went to Mrs. Almond's and learnt that the prisoner was staying at a coffee-house. Detective-Sergeant Monaghan found her there, and that she had on a silk necktie, one of the Missing articles. He had heard of a man finding a bundle containing a num- ber of articles, and which had been thrown over a wall. He found that some of these had Mrs. Pilkington's name on, and the prisoner admitted that she had stolen them and thrown them away. There were other articles not recovered. The prisoner, he understood, had been in a Reformatory. She was remanded till Monday. • THEFT BY A BOY.

At the Borough Police Court on Wednesday, before Alderman Holmes and Mr. J. Fairclough, Arthur Wood- house, a boy, aged 13, of 16, Howard-st., was charged with stealing from the wire-testing room at the White- cross works where he was employed, about six o'clock on Sunday night, three testing gauges, the pro- perty of the Whitecross Wire and Iron Co., Limited.— Jas. Hough deposed that he locked up one of the gauges about 12 o'clock on Saturday, and on Monday morning it was missing.—Mr. Birchall said the gauges, which were worth about £2 each, were locked up together The prisoner's brother,a boy employed at the works,had sent one of the gauges by one of the wiredrawer's sons to his father to offer him it for Is. 6d. This led to prisoner's detection. He stated that he came on Sunday to the works and that he and another lad were in the ware- house,'and opened the desk withthe key, which was lying under some papers ; when he heard somebody coming and ran off with two gauges, while the other lad took another, but threw it down. The latter boy now con- firmed the statement as to himself. Mr. Birchall said the gauge this boy stated he had thrown down had not been recovered. He desired only a slight punishment for the prisoner,as the company did not desire to blight a young life. Woodhouse was sentenced to receive six strokes of the birch rod that morning and six more in the evening.
A THANKLESS YOUNG SCAMP.

At the Borough Police Court, on Saturday, John Chas. Rowe, aged 14, an illegitimate child, and an orphan, Was charged with stealing a silver watch, value 155., the property of Elizabeth Stirrup, 66, Buttermarket-street. He pleaded guilty.—Chief Constable Hunt said the boy had been adopted by Mrs. Stirrup, when he was three months old, and kept by her till he was nine years of age, when he went somewhat wrong, and became irre- claimable. The parochial authorities then took him in hand, and placed him in the Catholic Schools, where he remained till February last. Then he became an errand boy, his last place having been at the Nag's Head, but he had to be got rid of there, as his employer could do no good with him. Mrs. Stirrup still allowed him to go to her home sometimes, and he was there on Tuesday afternoon. The watch was then in a box upstairs, as she supposed. she having last seen it there two or three months before. On Friday morning the prisoner sent a navvy into Mr. Houghton's, pawnbroker, to pawn a watch. Mr. Houghton asked the navvy where he got it, and he said a lad outside gave him it to pawn. Mr. 'Houghton went out to the prisoner, who told him that the watch had been left him by his grandfather, whobad died in Manchester some months before. The watch was subsequently identified as that of prosecutrix, and the lad given into custodv.—The Chairman, after reproach- ing the prisoner for his ingratitude to his benefactress, sentenced him, on his pramising to do better in future, to receive twelve strokes of the birch rod.
THE THEFT FROu A LOCK-TIP SHOP.

At the Warrington Borough Police Cou-ri:Oi; Saturday, Michael Garity, bricksetter's labourer, 4, Glasshouse- yard, and James Bibby, a shoemaker, living at Daley's lodging-house, 37, Scotland-road, were brought up on remand, charged with stealing from the lock-up shop of James Harper, shoemaker, 123, Sankey-st., some time between 9 p.m. on the 3rd inst. and 6.30 a m, on the 4th inst., a man's ooat, three pairs of boots, a bass, and a quantity of tools, value in all £2. Chief Constable Hunt said entry had been obtained to the premises by taking i out a large square of glass. Bibby had been n My. Harper's employ about ten days and then been dis- charged. Evidence was given by Thomas Cox, appren- tice to Mr. Harper, and Mrs. Leslie and Mts. Gibbon, the wives of dealers in Mersey-st. ; the two women deposing to the purchase of some of the articles on the morning of the 4th inst. Detective-Sergeant Monaghan deposed to apprehending the two men on the night of the 4th, and Bibby said Garity was innocent. On witness asking them about two pairs of boot not recovered by him, Garity said Bibby had told him they were hidden in the Park. Bibby said they were there near the rails, and witness found them there. Bibby now again pleaded guilty,and Garity not guilty. Bibby exculpated Garity, saying that he had nothing to do with the theft, and on being asked by him to pawn a pair of boots, re- fuscd, and left him saying he had been long enough with him.—Ganty : I thought they were stolen.—The pri- soners were committed for trial to the Quarter Sessions.
A,GANG OF DISREPUTABLE FEMALES.
On Thursday morning, --at Borough Police Alderman Sutton (chairman) and Captain Ridgway, Elizabeth Ellen Fleming (32nd appearance), Elizabeth

Brown, Winifred Jennings (7th appearance), Ann Holmes I (9th appearance), Annie Daly- (29th appearance), and ' Alice Thomas (16th appearance), all young women, were charged with indecent behaviour in Buttermarket-st., at half-past eleven the previous night.—lnspector Spinks said the bad language and disorderly behaviour of the prisoners was not fit to be mentioned in court. He, with the assistance of other constables, surrounded them and took them all into custody, except Fleming and Daley, who got away, hut were apprehended the same night. Fleming had her clogs in her hand, and was run- ning in her stocking feet. He had repeatedly cautioned these girls of late. They all lived in one house in Nay- lor-st.—The Chief Constable said they lived in Mrs. Ellen 13urke's lodging-house; in reply to Alderman Sutton stating that it was registered for seven.—Alderman Sut- ton: I doubt whether they would allow registration for a house of that sort.—Mr. Hunt said Mrs. liurke would not have any men there, that was, a man might take a jug of ale and pay for a gallon or two, but there was no going upstairs or anything of that sort. He wished the house could be broken up altogether as regarded harbouring this lot.—Alderman Sutton: Well, it a matter that will have to be taken into consideration, at any rate.—P.C. Bell corroborated the Inspector's evi- dence. He stated that Fleming and Brown commenced fighting, and fell to the ground, and the other four pri- soners came running out of Naylor-st.—D.S. Monoghan gave confirmatory testimony, and said the prisoners were both thieves and prostitutes.—Mr. Hunt urged that they should be bound over, so that in default of finding sureties they might have to lie in jail for a thne. They were [a disgrace, he said, to their sex. Walking day was coming on. Next Saturday (to-day) would be a busy day, and summer was coming on, and these girls could be well spared till October.—All the girls pleaded guilty, but Fleming said she had her clogs off because she was running away from a man, and did not want him to know where she was running to.—They were each sent to prison for a month's hard labour, the chair- man stigmatising them as a pest to society and a dis- grace to the town.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.

SATIIRDAY.—Before Alderman Chandley (chairman), Alderman Burgess, and Mr. J. White. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY. —Thomas Davey wa s charged with being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-street, the previous night, also with assaulting Patrick Clark, cab driver, the same night. A constable having proved the first charge, the defendant pleaded that he had been to Newton Races. The officer, he said, tore his waist- coat to ribbands. The cab driver stated that he was standing in the Patten Arms, being employed by Mrs. Kiernan, when the defendant, who was standing at the door, said, "Is that Irish Paddy ?" and "up with his stick, and sent my hat flying, split in two—(laughter)— and sent me right to the floor." The hat was the same that Mr. Hunt gave him. He had never wronged the defendant in his life. The defendant said the prosecutor should go and bring the hat, and let the magistrates see it. Witness had been horse-keeper at the place before ever the prosecutor was there. He had a drop of drink, and just gave the man's hat a shove.—Mr. Hunt said the defendant was becoming a perfect nuisance.—Clara said the case would not have been brought, had not the defendant been caught in the stalls about midnight, punching a horse in the "guts." The defendant was fined 10s. and costs; in default 14 days' imprison- ment.

WIFE ASSAULT.—James Wright was charged with as- saulting his Wife Ann, on the 29th ult., and was bound over in the sum of £5 to keep the peace for six months, and ordered to pay the costs, 135., the Chairman in- forming his wife that as the law was she could leave him when she thought proper, if he abused her again. _ _
MONDAY—Before the Afarir (Aid. R. W. Franconih) and
Aldeiman Sutton.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—John Rooney, drunk and disorderly in Bridge-st., on Saturday night, was fined 10s., including costs.—William Rayner, drunk and dis- orderly and refusing to quit the licensed premises of John Evans, the Bull's Head Inn, on Saturday night, was I fined 205. and costs.—John Heaton was charged with be- ing drunk and disorderly in Hill-st., on Saturday night, and with assaulting P.C. Bell and William Burrows the same night. The officer deposed that the prisoner was drunk and maxing a disturbance in a house in Hill-st., and he put him out, and told him to go away, which he did. Some time after witness was called to the same place, and found the prisoner assaulting an old man who was blind. Witness put him outside, and, as he refused to go away, took him into custody. Heaton assaulted him on the way to the station, and when Mr. Burrows came to his assistance struck him twice. A woman named Bridget Mooney, a lodger at the house from which the prisoner was ejected, testified to his disorderly con- duct, and said that he gave her two black eyes. Mr. Burrows having given evidence, Heaton was sentenced to two months' imprisonment with hard labour.—John McDonald, drunk and disorderly in Buttermazket-st., on Saturday night, was fined 105. including costs.—James Carr, drunk and disorderly in Winwick-st., on 2nd inst, ; and Michael Mulcairn, in Crown and Septre Yard, onfthe Ist inst, discharged. WIFE DEst RTION. illiam Whitfield, 48, Cartwright- st., was charged with deserting his wife Sarah Ann Whit- field, 44, Rose and Crown-st ,on the 19th May. Mr. P. Davies appeared for the complainant,and Mr. A. Browne for the defendent. Mr. Davies said the parties were married on August 2nd, 1880, and by mutual agreement lived with her father,but about two months ago the hus- band took the things away and stayed away until the 19th of May, when he came and took their boy, seven years of age, away, and she went and brought the child back. There was not accommodation for her where he was now ' living.—Mr. Browne said that was only a temporary I place, and he had done his utmost to get a ouse but could not. He was anxious to get her out of the district ,of Rose and Crown-st.--In reply to Mr. Browne, Mr. Davies said the defendant was such a good husband that his wife did not want to part with him.—The case was adjourned for a fortnight to allow him a chance of ob- taining a house. FIGHTING.—Patrick Kenealy and Patrick Quinn, for fighting in Bridge-st., on the 30th ult., were bound over in each other's rec,-Inizances of £5 to keep the peace for six months, and ordered to pay the costs, ss. each. FITCH AND Toss.—John Titchett, Eiwa.rd Wal MR ley, and William Lee, boys, for playing at pitch and toss in Turner-st., on Sunday last, were fined 25. ad. each. CHIMNEYS ON FIRE. Frank Cashinelli, ice cream dealer Fennell-st.. and Henry Isherwood, Howley Lane, were fined is. each for having their chimneys on fire. TUESDAY.—Before Mr. R. Garnett (chairman),and Mr. E.

div.head: J. Guest.
div.p: J. Guest.
WIFE ASSAULT.—Johtcltwi, for assaulting his wife Jane on Sunday, was blund over in the sum of £5 to keep the peace for six months, sad ordered to pay the costs, Bs. 6d.
DRUNK AND DISORDRRLY.—Patrick Garrity, drunk and disorderly in Horsemarket-st., on Monday night, was fined_ss. including costs.

r, A WANDERING LUNATIC.—George Cank WAS charged with wandering in Wilderspool-road, on Monday night, he being of unsound mind.—lnspector Spinks said the defendant stated that he belonged to Gateshead and that he was there at the present time. His wife,he said.lived in Gateshead, and if they would let him go he would have his breakfast with her in a few minutes.—ln reply to the Chairman the defendant said Gateshead was only five miles from there. He was now in wcastle. He had often been in Warrington. It was five miles from Widnes. He was not in Gateshead now but in Northumberland. He was told he was in Warrington.—The defendant was ordered to be handed over to the Relieving Officer. SCHOOL Cesgs.—The following cases were dealt with at the instance of Mr. George Riley :—John Broad, rail- way servant, Timothy Egan, tanner, Dial-st., John Fallon, labourer, Ship Yard, Peter Fallon, labourer, Crossley-st., and James Travis, forgeman,Silver-square, 2 6d. each.—Ellen Carter, labourer, Friars Green. in whose case a Friendly Society had been paying the school fee, and whose child had only made 95 out of a possible 150 attendances, John Carr, labourer, Dial-st., Thomas Harrison, labourer, Winwick-st., and Lawrence Lyden,tanner,Crossley-st.,ls. each. Jonas Finn,labourer, Cockhedge, Thomas Rider, and Wm. Burton, forgemen, of Bewsey-road, ss. each.—John Lee, forgeman. Pior- point-st., had an order made against him.for his daugh- ter to be sent to the Elizabeth Industrial School, Liver- pool. The child's father objected to this, promising to send the girl regularly to school if the Bench would allow him another chance.—The Chairman: We will make no alteration. It will be the best thingfor her. FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison and Mr. It. Garnett.
DRUNK.—Annie West, charged with being drunk on Cropper's Brow, on the 28th of April, 1890, was, on the recommendation of the Chief Constable, dismissed. _ _

CHARGE OF THREATENING A WIFE.--JOsenh Lowe, coal dealer, 15, Derby-street, was charged by his wife, Maria Frances Lowe, with using threatening language to her on Saturday last, The complainant said she had been obliged to go home to her father six weeks since in consequenee of his threats, and had remained from home five weeks. The case was adjourned four weeks te allow the parties to come to an amicable understanding if possible.

- NON-SUPPORT OF A Sow.—Henry Goodhead, 18 Atherton's Quay, charged with not contributing for the maintenance of his .on on board the Clio, had an order made against him for payment of 2.5. 6d. per week. CRURLTY TO ANIMALS.—InSpeCtOT Doughty, of the R. S.P.C.A ~ prosecuted in the following cases :—Frederick Chadwick, a boy, of 3 Rowe-st., was charged with cruelly treating, abusing, and torturing an ass attached to a cart of flour, by violently beating it in Priestly-st., on the 27th ult. and was fined ss• including costs.—Edward Bate, Church-st., was charged with cruelly treating a horse attached to a bus he was driving at Market Gate, on the 29th ult., by violently striking the animal. He was ordered to pay the costs, 3s. 6d. WlFit DESERTION.—Richard Higham, fustian cutter, 20, Watkin-st., was charged with deserting his wife Alice Higham and refusing to maintain her. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the defence, and stated that the defendant paid 10A. a week for her maintenance in the workhouse. —Alderman Harrison: He cannot do that. The work- house is not a lodging-house. It is the duty of the man to provide a home for her.—Mr. Brownel:—We have got a home all the time.—The complainant said the defend- ant did not mean to have her at home. She had gone at ten o'clock at night, and be had refused to admit her.

PADGATE WESLEYANS 17. WARRINGTON ABUT/MS.- 1 his match should have been played at Padgate on Satur- day, but owing to the state of the weather it was can- celled.

WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH CHOIR V. BRICK-STREET SUNDAY ScHooL.—This match was played on the Choir ground and resulted in a win for the:visitors by 15 runs. Score :—Brick-st., 37, Parish Church Choir 22. Hamp- son fcr the home team did good service with the ball, capturing nine wickets at the cost of a few runs. RUNCORN TRINITY CHURCH V. BALFOUR INSTITUTE.— Played at Greenbank on Saturday. The home eleven went first to bat, Cauche being the only one to make any stand against the deliveries of Heath and Challis,all being out for 31. When_Trinity's four wickets fell the issue was beyond doubt, but the remaining six wickets offered very little resistance, the total only reaching 40. Score :—Balfour's, 31; Trinity, 40. CADISHRAD AND IRLADI v. BESWICH.—rhis match was played at Cadishead, and formed the benefit of Alfred Davies. The day was rather unpropitious, but notwith- standing this many visited the ground. The Congrega- tional Saud came on the field and played at intervals. The game did not commenteuntil 3.40, and then Beswick went in. Play opened badly for them, for by Isaac Arstall's first ball bit's wickets were spread-eagled by a yorker. Arstall, however, did no more damage, as in fielding a ball he received an abdominal sprain, which eventually necessitated him leaving the field. L. Taylor and J. Wrigley then bowled unchanged, and disposed of their opponents for 53 runs. On Cadishead going in they were favoured with the best light and scored very rapidly, making 61 runs for eight wickets in 75 minutes. Thanks to smart wicket-keeping on both sides, each team only obtained one extra. WIDNES V. ST. HELENS RECREATION.—PIayed at Widnes on Saturday. Score : WIDNES. RECREATION. WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. LONGFORD MANURE WORKS. The monthly meeting of this Authority was held at the Workhouse, yesterday week. Mr. R. Heaton pre- sided, and there were also present Messrs. Dobson, Swin- ton, Humphreys, J. Houghton, Smith, Mather, W. Houghton, Jolley; S. Sutton (clerk), W. Owen (sur- veyor), Dr. Sephton (medical officer), and F. Kerfoot (inspector). Nxw HOUSES, &c.—The Surveyor submitted the fol- lowing plans for approval :—Additions to the works of the Mersey White Lead Co., Sankey Bridges; eight houses at Glazebrook, for Mr. Joseph Bridge ; new hoase at Hepherd's Farm, Woolston Moss, for Mr. W. Bennett; alterations and additions to the Friends' School, Pen- keth. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.—INFLUENZA.—Dr. Seph- ton reported that there had been 22 births and 30 deaths in the district during the past month. The drath rate was equal to 221 per 1,000, as compared with 12.3 during the last three months, and 11.6 during the same period last year. The death rate was very high for that district, the cause being chest diseases after influenza, and convulsions in teething. LONGFORD MANURE.—The Inspector reported that he had had numerous complaints of a nuisance in Orford arising from middens of offensive manure on land in the occupation of three farmers. The manure was excreta, which had been carted in a tank by the Warrington Cor- poration from the Longford depot and deposited on the land of the farmers referred to.—The Inspector, in ans- wer to a question, said the Cprporation were overstocked with the manure, and were giving it to the farmers.— Mr. Swinton said he had heard some very strong com- plaints of the nuisance. Many people were made sick in going past it.—Mr. Mather corroborated Mr. Swinton as to the effects of the nuisance.—The Chairman said the Corporation were giving the manure to the farmers, and the farmers were taking it as fast as possible.—lt was decided to give seven days' notice for an abatement of the nuisance. This was all the business.
WARRINGTON BANKRUPTCY COURT.
Yesterday week before Mr. Registrar Nicholson.

A BANKRUPT NEWSAGENT.—WiIIiam Savory, newsagent and general dealer, of 44, Ellesmere-st., Warrington, ap- peared to undergo his public examination. A receiving order was made against the debtor on his petition on the 29th of April, and on the same day he was adjudged bankrupt. Savory, in his statement to the Official Re- ceiver, stated that he was an overlooker in a cotton mill by trade. About 1880 he opened a news- paper shop in Church-st., Warrington. He had about £3O capital of his own. About 1887, he removed to 72, Church-st., where he also carried on the business of general dealer. In November, 1889, a fire on the pre- mises destroyed his stock and furniture, which was not insured. A few friends collected nearly £1,5 to enable him to continue his business, which he did up to threel months ago. He was now working in a mill as an over- looker, and his wife kept on the shop. The deficiency amounted to £177 4s. 11d., and of that sum he esti- mated that £l3O was lost in consequence of the fire. There were no assets except book debts, estimated to produce £2.—The examination was adjourned for a fort- night. A BOOT DEALER'S TROUBLES.—Abraham John Ward, shoe manufacturer, late of Marston-road, Stafford, now residing at 275, Knutsford-rd.,Latchford, was also exam- ined. A receiving order was made against the bankrupt on his own petition, on the Bth ult. The deficiency was pot down at £135175. 10d., and the assets were nil. The Assistant-Official Receiver characterised the deficiency account as an eminently unsatisfactory one, and the debtor promised to endeavour to furnish further par- ticulars.—The examination was adjourned. TEURSDAY.—Before his Honor Judge Ffoulkes. CAESE LIST.—The cause list at this court contained 4 adjourned plaints, 4 default summonses, 109 original plaints, and 31 judgment summonses. THE STATUTE OF LIMITATIONS BARRED. —Mr. Moulding, solicitor, Liverpool, applied to his Honor for costs to be allowed to his client, Mr. T. C. Pierpoint, who was formerly an architect residing in Warrington, but at the present time lived at Liscard. The application was made on the ground that the plaintiff, Mr. Adam G. Webster, tailor, Buttermarket-st., had commenced an action against Mr. Pierpoint for £24 for work done and materials supplied ten years ago. Defendant had pleaded the Statute of Limitations, and the plaintiff had given notice of discontinuance only on Tuesday last. He, therefore, asked that costs be allowed.—His Honor said he could see no objection.—Mr. Arthur Browne, who was for the plaintiff, said that it was a tailor's bill for clothes supplied to the defendant by the plaintiff over ten years ago. After contracting the debt, defendant went away to South Africa, and had only lately returned to this country. Naturally enough, plaintiff applied for payment of his account, and defendant's reply was to plead the Statute of Limitations. He asked his Honor to exercise discretion and say that defendant ought not to have costs.—His Honor said the defendant had, legally, a perfect right to Ale such a defence, and lie could not see any reason why he should depart from the ordinary custom, which was to grant costs.—Mr. Browne said he asked it on moral grounds.—His Honor made an order against the plaintiff for the payment of costs up to the time of discontinuing the action. I TAILOR'S CLAna.—Johr. Mawson, trading as Mawson and Co., tailor, Sankey-st., Warrington, sued a young man named Henry Grace, of Winwick -road, for £4 45., the price of an overcoat. The plaintiff was represented by Mr. Forshaw. The plaintiff said defendant ordered an overcoat,the price of which was fixed at three guineas, but as he afterwards ordered several extras an extra guinea had to be charged. Defendant argued that the original price was to include all that Mr. Mawson de- scribed as extras. A verdict was given for the plaintiff for the amount claimed.

CLAIM Br A LANDLORD. W. J. Legh claimed £5 12s. 61. from Mrs. E. A. Lane, of Newton, as executrix of her late husband Mr. John Lane, for occupation rent of land in Birley-st., Newton for three- quarters of a year from the 29th September, 1889. A counter-claim for £7 146. was put in by the defendant which contained solicitors charges for carrying out in- structions given by plaintiff's agent in respect to lease, for journeys to Warrington, for extra stamp duty, &c. Mr. A. Browne, of Warrington, appeared for the plaintiff. Mr. Pardy, agent for the plaintiff, and Mr. Clarke, sur- veyor, were called in support of the claim: A verdict was given for the plaintiff on both the claim and the counter-claim.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
CRICKET.

There was a marvellous change in the cricket shown by the Notts and Middlesex elevens at Lords on Tuesday from that displayed by the same teams on Monday. Middlesex on Monday fielded wretchedly and batted without any life or power, while the Notts intn batted capitally and acquitted themselves creditably in the other departments of the game. On Tuesday, on the other hand, the home side batted very finely and, setting Notts 134 to get to win, actually got the whole ten wickets down in less than two hours for 84, the game thus ending in a• brilliant and altogether unexpected victory for Middlesex by 49 runs. Of course, the South- country team would have had no chance of victory with- out the excellent batting of Johnston, Rawlin,and West, but even when Middlesex had put together 233 they looked to have little or no chance of succcess, for the wicket was still in capital condition. Hearne and Nepean, however, bowled in rare form, and, backed up by some admirable fielding, they had six wickets down in less than an hour for 27 rums. Nepean took four wickets for 22 and Hearne four for 35, making the former's record eight wickets for 87 runs and the latter's nine for 98.

Several county players who were released by the abandonment of the Kent match did good service in other places on Saturday. Frank Sugg scored 62, Paul 45 (not out), Baker 40, and Barlow 20 (not out). Yates put in an appearance at Old Trafford, greatly to the ad- vantage of the Manchester Club, who were not doing very well against the Whalley Range bowlers. He scored 50, and was then driven on to his wicket by one of Mr. Jones's throws. The wicket seemed to suit Irving, and he bowled with great success.

Lohmann's birthday occurred last week—he was born, says Dr. Grace, in Kensington, on June 5, 1865—and the famous Surrey man celebrated the occasion by a fine performance against Gloucestershire. In the record of the two Gloucestershire innings his name occurs no fewer than twelve times.

Several of the oldest cricketers in the country declare they cannot remember such a wet season as we are now having. It must be simply ruinous to those club who have not a big balance to fall back upon, while the caterers at the big grounds begin to wish they had never been born.

The Notts and Yorkshire County Clubs must begin to see the folly ot not finding some employment for their young players instead of allowing them to go afield for employment and locating themselves elsewhere. If Notts could secure all the leading players born in their county they would have a tremendous Eleven—one capable of playing England, in fact. Take, for instance, the fol- lowing :—Shrewsbury, Gunn, Dixon, Barnes, Flowers, Attewell, Briggs, Sharpe, Lockwood, Bean, and Sher- win. Why don't both counties follow the example of Surrey and Lancanshire, and start a club and ground Even poor Sussex has one.

The advantage obtained by Lancashire over Leicester- shire at Leicester on Monday was well followed up on Tuesday, and by five minutes to four the visitors had gained a victory by seven wickets. Some such result was expected from the overnight state of the game, as Leiceitershire, with ten wickets to fall in their second innings, were still .43 runs behind. On resuming on Tuesday morning the home team started wonderfully well. Wheeler and Tomlin raised the overnight total of 19 to 38 for the first wicket, and then the latter with Warren added 19 for the second wicket. From this point, however, the batting broke down, and the remaining eight wickets fell for an addition of 43. Warren batted in good form, and his 33 was the second highest individual score in the match. Briggs again proved the most successful Lancashire bowler, and in the two innings he had the fine record of twelve wickets for 66 runs. Lancashire required 39 to win, and so well were Pougher and Walton supported in the field that the runs occupied 65 minutes in getting and cost three wickets.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

The "Athletic News" says :—" That was indeed a popular selection the Warrington footballers arrived at when H. Ashton was returned unopposed for the cap- taincy for 1891. H. Ashton, in the opinion of not a few, is the only competent person in the club for so respon- sible a position."

The Lancashire Football Combination has been duly launched, and we have another addition to the long la of organisations uhder the League system. The Com- bination clubs are a very level lot, and the League Re- serve teams are very sensible to go together. The names of the clubs are as follow :—Blackburn Rovers, Bolton Wanderers, Burnley and Darwen Reserves, Halliwell, North Meols, Hindley, Skeimersdale United, Royton, Irwell Springs, and Brierfield.

The West Lancashire Rugby champions are mourning the loss of one of their best forwards. This was William Williamson, who, whilst working at the Bridgewater Colliery's No. 3 Pit, was killed by a fall of roof. He was only 23 years of age. His coffin was carried to its last resting place by his old clubmates, and there was much sorrowing in the village. On the very morning of his death the poor fellow was talking about the medal he was to receive as one of the winners of the West Lanca- shire Cup.

div.head: WELSH TRAGEDY.
div.p: THE WELSH TRAGEDY.

On enquiry at the Benar View Hotel, Dolbyddelen, on Thursday night it was stated that Mrs. Duncan was a good deal better, and that the wounds in the head had almost closed, and in a month would probably be healed LIP as much as it is possible they can be. Mr. Duncan's mental condition, however, cannot as yet be said to be improving.

div.head: REVENGEFUL MODEL.
div.p: A REVENGEFUL MODEL.

On Wednesday,at Dublin,a young man named Hunter, was sentenced for his revengeful things at the studio of Miss Redmond, where he had been acting as model. For malicious injury to a statue lie was ordered two years', for causing bodily harm to Miss Redmond ,five years',and for the theft at her studio, seven years' penal servitude, the sentences to be concurrent.

div.head: TWO YOUTHS DROWNED.
div.p: TWO YOUTHS DROWNED.

George Clement Knox Fletcher and his brother, Hugh Somerset, sons of the Rev. J. Knox Fletcher, of Whittle. bury Rectory, Towchester, and students of Trinity Col- lege, Stratford-on-Avon, were drowned on Wednesday afternoon, while bathing in the Avon, about two miles below Stratford. One of the deceased was sixteen and the other seventeen years of age.

Reunions PILLs.—A trade mark action of considerable public interest and importance came before Mr. Justice Kekewich on Saturday. Messrs. Holloway, of 78, New Oxford Street, London, the well-known proprietors of Holloway's Pills and Ointment, had become aware that penny boxes of pills called Elolloway's Pills were being offered for sale, although the proper retail price is one shilling and three halfpence per box. On analysing the pills sold, Messrs. Holloway found that the pills were not manufactured by them at all, and accordingly brought an action in the High Court of Justice to restrain Mr. James Best, a chemist and druggist, from selling any pills as Holloway's Pills which were not really made by them. No defence having been put in, Mr. Israel Davis, on behalf of Messrs. Holloway, applied to Mr. Justice Kekewich for an injunction, and Counsel for the Defen- dant admitting he could not resist the motion, a per- petual injunction was granted restraining the acts com- plained of, and further awarding to Messrs. Holloway damages and all costs. The appeal.by the prosecutors of the Bishop of Lincoln against the main part of the Primate's judgment was begun before the Judicial Committee on Wednesday. ARE THE INTERCEPTING DEPOTS A 'NUISANCE ? .

Sir,—Knowing the difficult duty the .Sanitary Com- mittee have to perform in clearing away the excreta from the town, I would be the last man to add to their difficulties by complaining, but when Alderman Platt, at the Coned!. Meeting on Tuesday, when discussing the question of insanitary dwellings, said "he wished the Sanitary Committee would extend their vigilance a little further, and consider the question of the Intercept- ing Depots in Lvthgoes Lane, which smelled badly that afternoon," wasi told by a councillor that such a thing was "impossible," I -think I ought to confirm what Alderman Platt said by stating that several times re- cently, and for two days last week, the stench arising from the Howley Depot is sickening to the last degree. Town Councillors who do not reside in the neighbour- hood of these depots, and who never come near them, should at least refrain from expressing so decided an opinion.—Yours truly, Warrington, June 4th, 1891.
S. DAVIES.

[lt was Councillor Pierpoint who exclaimed "Impos- sible !"; but his tone and manner showed that he used the word ironically. He was one of the few who voted the other day for an inquiry into the nuisance of the Depots.—Ed. Ex.

div.head: "NEUTRAL GREENS."
div.p: "NEUTRAL GREENS."

Sir,—The Lancashire and Cheshire Bowling Association have had their meeting, and decided to play the compe- tition matches on neutral greens! The majority that brought that decision about may be clever, but they are not clever enough to find a neutral green anywhere with- in 30 miles of Manchester. What I mean by neutral greens is: that they shall be greens about which the competing teams shall know nothing, and so meet on even terms. The farce of this was exemplified when on several occasions, in the years gone by, some of the competitors knew every inch of the ground they had to play on, whilst their opponents saw the green on the match day for the first time. ' Andthey think this fair! and equitable ! ! It is perfectly plain that a sense of grief and disappointment has had the mastery over those clubs who were beaten last year. and has prompted them to want a plan by which they can get "nearer home!" But what an exhibition of cowardice it dis- plays! And what a high compliment—if an unprofitable one—for those who could beat them on their own sod, and of whom they are so manifestly afraid Sir, the wit of man can devise only one fair way of playing these games, namely, home and home. Another may, and has been tried, but the wayfarer, who is not a fool," c,an see that it was and must of necessity be us- /air; and will in the end "kill the imaginary goose that lays the golden eggs "—or in other words, will damn the Association and all its go id works) Warrington, sth June, 1891.

Sir,—! much regret that I am under the necessity of addressing you in order to refute a foul slander. Mr. Battersby, speaking at the Conservative meeting on Wednesday night,said my workshop was a" black shop," and that "anyone who belonged to the trade,and worked at the shop would be immediately expelled the Society." Now, I challenge Mr. Battersby to try to make good his assertion ; and I offer to give £lO to the Infirmary if he proves his words, on condition that he will give £lO to the Infirmary if he fails to prove them. As I stated at the meeting I addressed, on Monday night, I was, when working at the anvil, one of the pro- moters of the Union of workmen in the tool trade in the neighbourhood of Rainhill, and it resulted in a revised list and higher prices. I am anxious now, as I was then, to give assistance in revis- ing prices in the tool trade; and, as I stated on Mon- day night, I will help either the men in this matter, or the Warringtp Trades Council. Could any employer say more? It Is as false as anything can be to suggest that! have anything to do with " sweating," or that I do not pay the usual wages of the trade. But let Mr. Battersby accept my challenge, and the truth will soon be known. .
As you will. I presume, be reporting the speech which so grossly misrepresents me, I trust that.in justice to myself, you will make room for this reply in your next issue.—Yours faithfully,
GEO. PLIMPTON. 12.5, Lovely-law, Warrington, June 11, 1891.
CAPITAL PUNISHMENT.

Sir,—! was considerably surprised to read in the "Examiner" the other day your statement that a Mr. Charles Scott had adduced statistics in the "Juridical Review" showing that wherever the death penalty had been altogether or almost abolished murder had in- creased in an extraordinary degree. You say, too, that he cites the cases of Belguim, Prussia, and Switzerland,

as instances in point. This is so startlingly contrary to most that I have read on the subject of capital punish- ment for many years past, and the question is one of such supreme importance that I ask your permission to use your columns for the purpose of presenting some statistics which are diametrically opposed to those of Mr. Scott. These were contributed by the well-known writer" Vera x "to the "Manchester Weekly Times" in December 1883 or January 1884; and, I have his article now before me. According to it, the facts

stood as follows: In Holland the punishment of death was abolished in IMO, and the Minister of Justice in that country stated in 1880 that dur- ing the period from 1861 to 1869, inclusive, there were 19 murders, while fromll37l to 1879 there had been but 17, though the population had increased. In Belgium capital punishment was Dractically abolished, being formally retained, but never having been carried out since 1863, yet, while for the 17 years from 1847 to 1863 there were 183 sentences of deaths for murder, in the 17 years from 1863 to 1880 there were only 128 convictions of murder, 55 fewer than during the hanging, period. In America capital punishment had been abolished in Michigan, Wisconsin, Rhode Island, and Maine, and there had been no concurrent increase of murder. In Michigan, since .1847, when the death penalty was abrogated there, murder had, allowing for the increase of population, diminished by 50 per cent. As to Switzerland the facts arecited that though—capital punishment having been abolished there by a decree in 1879—the cantons recovered the right of re-establishing the penalty as law, and seven of them had exercised this right, yet, nothwithstanding this, down .to February, 1883, no sentence of death had been passed in any of them. In the remaining fifteen cantons, comprising more than four-fifths of the population of the republic, I he law of capital punishment had not been re-established. The presumption, therefore, would seem to be, though Verax " does not state whether this had been the case, that Switzerland had not experienced any increase in the number of murders through the abolition of the death punishment. I have certainly read somewhere that such an increase has taken place in that country, but that this is due to the fact that most of the murders in Switzerland are committed during intoxication, so that the conditions causing murders in that country would not be affected by the change in the law. In Finland, when " Verax" wrote, there had been no execution since 1824, yet the Judge of the Court of Appeal in that country reported that the security of person and property had not been in the least diminished, and murders were extremely rare. Now, even supposing Switzerland to be an excep- tion to that rule, it seems pretty eertain from " Verax's" statement that up to the end of 1883 or beginning of 1844, in every other part of the wotld where death had ceased to be the punishment for murder the number of murders had diminished.

" Verax " states that he derives most of his figures from the publications of that high authority on the sub- ject, the'lloward Association. That being so, they can- not very well be discredited ; and, with all deference to Mr. Scott, I am strongly disinclined to believe that humanity ' the world over has become so much more wicked of late that the conditions " Arerax " describes have been completely reversed during the past seven years.

But " Verax " takes the converse sid6' of the question, and shows that in England where capital punishment had been so rigorously preserved, murders had gone on increasing, there having been from 1850 to 1859, 167 con- victions for murder in this country, while between 1870 and 1879 there were 255, an increase of 88, though popu- lation had increased to nothing like corresponding extent. I might add to " Verax's" statements the fact that in Italy, where capital punishment prevails, there are more murders than in all the other great nations of Europe put together. In 1878—I am going rather far back, but have not later statistics—the combined popu- lation of France, Germany, Spain, England, Ireland, and Scotland was something like 130 millions, and they had amongst them 2,243 murderers. In Italy, during the same year with a population of only 27 millions, there were 2,574 murderers. Judging from recent revelations, it;is probable that an even worse state of things prevails in that country now. The existence, and frequency, of capital punishment in France seems to be small deterrent from the commission of murder in that country, if one may juege from the appalling accounts one reads of the diabolically deliberate assassinations which are so numer- ous there. It might be argued that this is because so many convicted murderers in France escape the guillo- tine on account of the proverbial readiness of French courts at discovering extenuating circumstances. But, that class of murders for which no extenuation can be foundeven in France is not only not on the decrease., but decidedly on the increase there. I could pursue this subject much further from a moral and philosophical standpoint ; but I have already en- croached on your space. I may.couclude by saying that the question is not one to be settled by any concise aphorism or offhand generality,: such as some seem to think so conclusive, but, being a problem of life and death, demands the most careful and profound consider- ation, and exhaustive discussion.—Yours
MANLIUS.

div.head: TRE VYRNWY SUPPLY.
div.p: TRE VYRNWY SUPPLY.
THE TEMPORARY PIPE LAID.

Although it was fully expected that the Vyrnwy water supply would be through at l'rescot on Saturday, that anticipation was not realised. A telegram received by Mr. Parry, the waterengineer, from Fidler's Ferry, stated that the junction of the temporary pipe line had not been effected on the Lancashire side of the Mersey in conse- querce of the weather. Meanwhile, at Prescot a large gang of men have been at work clearing out the reservoir preparatory to receiving the new supply. On Thursday night, however, the connection was com- pleted, and the Vyrnwy water was ready to be sent through the pipes to Prescot whenever the arrangements there have been perfected. On the Cheshire side, the temporary pipe, 24in. in diameter, is taken from the main pipe (421 n. at a distance of thirty yards from the Ship Canal bank, and is laid for about 150 yards parallel to the canal and toward Warrington. It is here opposite the temporary pipe across the river, and it is proposed to lay under the canal bed a pipe of 21in. diameter. The Ship Canal authorities insist that the 21in. pipe must be placed 4ft. under the bed of the canal, and as this requires 18ft. of further excavation in the soft running sand con- siderable delay must elapse before such a pipe can be placed at the required depth. Excavations are being proceeded with, but to meet the urgent demand for obtaining a supply of Vyrnwy water immediately in Liverpool a 15is. pipe has been placed in the present bed of the canal, which will seive the purpose until the lay- ing of the 21in. pipe has been completed. An incident which happened on the Cheshire shore dur- ing the launching of the river pipe was very near ending, in serious results to Mr. T. Kirby, the energetic superin- tendent of the temporary pipes. The pipe was about 81t. out of position as it was nearing the Cheshire shore, and Mr. Kirby and others were endeavouring to right it when the steam winch began to pull. The beam across the pipe caught Mr. Kirby, and knocked him down on his back in the mud, and there Ma him fast. The engine was promptly stopped, but as the heay beam and pipe were resting on Mr. Kirby's logs he was in great danger of being choked with the mud, or having his legs broken. He partly scrambled, and was partly pulled from his perilous position. _ _
The suggestion of the Warrington Corporation to place posts on each bank of the river, indicating the position of the sunken pipe, has been acted upon.
WATER AT LAST.

THE CONNECTION MADE Yi§filiDAY MORNING. A happy consummation was reached yesterday morn- ing. There is water from Vyrnwy at last. Liverpool may therefore hops that in a short time it will have the full benefit of the abundant supply that has so long been promised from the great Welsh reservoir. This, no doubt, is a hope that has been held out for a long time, and as frequently deferred; but now it is all but accomplished. This realisation is in a great measure owing to the skill. foresight, and energy of Mr. Parry, the water engineer, and his staff of able assistants. After much engineering ingenuity, labour, and no little danger, the temporary pipe line laid across the bed of the Mersey connecting the water pipes on the Cheshire side with those on the Lancashire shore were yesterday morning connected. All being ready, the tap was turned on at Oswestry reser- voir, and soon there was a mighty rush of water all along the pipe line. There were no leakages of any moment, and the water flowed freely through the sub- merged pipe line joining the Cheshire and Lancashire I shores to the reservoir at Prescot. Here, for the present, ' is the termination of the connection. The pipes being newly laid, require flushing to get rid of any objection- able matter that may have in the process of laying been ' deposited in them. For this purpwe there will be a steady flow of water along the pipe line from Oswestry to Prescot. As soon as the pipes have been sufficiently flushed immediate steps will be taken for the supoly to be taken to Liverpool. The quantity of water at Vyrnwy at pre- sent is enormous, and the opening up of the new supply to Liverpool at the present time will be most acceptable. The news of the Neater being let on was received with much satisfaction by the water authorities in Liverpool, the members of the Water Committee, and others who have been interested in this gigantic undertaking. The tunnel and pipe line under the Mersey, the construction of which is a work of great difficulty, is progressing favourably under the direction of Mr. Deacon, and in a very short time it is hoped Liverpool will have the full benefit of a copious water supply fcom Vyrnwy.

div.head: SUBWAY UNDER THE SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SUBWAY UNDER THE SHIP CANAL.

The subway for the permanent Vyrnwy pipe line under the Manchester Ship Canal was practically completed last week. The Manchester Ship Canal at Fidler's Ferry has only been partially excavated at this point. It will run parallel to the river, and will be separated by less than 100 yards from the Mersey. The length of the sub- way from the shaft on the Norton bank of the canal to the shaft on the bank next to the river is 304 feet, and its diameter is 122 feet. It is founded on concrete, vary- ing from one foot to eight feet in thickness. The base of tl.e subway is 20 feet under the proposed bed of the canal, and 45 feet below the ordinary water surface level of the canal. A hydraulic pump will be placed in the shaft on the Norton bank to remove any leakage water that may find its way into the subway. The main permanent pipe which has been laid down from Lake Vyrnwy to the Canal bank, a distance of about 60 miles, is of east-iron and of 42 inch diameter, but it is proposed to place a steel pipe of 36-inch diameter along the subway. MRS. Sc rGENEIII.,.

General Booth, the head 6f the Salvation Army, was born at Nottingham, nii_April 10th, 1829. 'He studied theology with the Rev. Wm. Cooke, D.D., became a minister ,of the Methodist New Connexion in 1850, and was appointed mostly to hold special evangelistic services, to which he felt so strongly drawn that when the Conference of .1861 required him to settle in the ordinanyecircuit work, he re- signed. He then began to labour amongst the churches as an evangelist wherever he had an op- portunity. Going in that capacity to the East end of London, le ebserve.d that the vast majority of the people attended no p!ace of worship, and he commenced "The Christian Mission" in July, 1865. To this Mission, when it had become a large organ- isation, formed upon military lines, he gave in 1878 the name of " The Salvation Army." To write the life of General Booth since that time would be to write the wonderfal history of the Salvation Army.. To the development of the Ariny has been devoted' not only his own life but the lives of all his family. "There have been," we are told, "great men and famous men who have founded great and world- wide organizations, but General Booth is the first one who has at the same time ,reared a family for the express purpose of carrying on and perfecting the work which he has begun." .Perhaps the secret is to be found in the fact that the Salvation Army is quite as much the work of his wife as it is of himself. The Salvation Army believes in heredity; it believes in training; and botltheliefs find strong- est confirmation in the extriordiaary capacity of the wholo family. Consecrated from the cradle to the service of the Army, they have without a single exception—and there are eight of them—devoted their lives to the cause. All differ, but all possess smile measure of the extraordinary gifts of their extraordinary parents. Physically they are far tfrom robus'z. There never was such a set of cripples who did such heavy work as the booth family. Mrs. Booth all her life through suffered from an nifection of the heart, which often prostrated her for hours after addressing a great meeting, and has repeatedly laid her aside for weeks together. Mrs. Booth-Clibborn, the Marshall of the French Salva- tion Army, suffers from weakness of the spine. Mr. Biainwell Booth for years was such a sufferer from heat t disease, left by rheumatic fever, that he could not lie down even to sleep. Mr. Herbert Booth suffers similarly. Weak and ailing though they are, they have an infinite reserve of energy and "go." Trained almost from childhood to handle all the practical details of administration and finance, accustomed every day to deal with men and women as individuals and in names, there is not a member of the, family now in the field who would not., if the occasion should unfortunately arise, be much better prepared to take over the duties of corn-1 mander-in-chief than General Booth twelve years ! ago seemed prepared for the direction of a great , world-wide religious organisation. The death of Mrs. Booth, "The Mother of the ISalvation Army," will be well within the memory of our readers. It took place on the 4th of October last, and her remains were laid to rest amid popular demonstrations in London almost unparalleled in our time.

div.head: DARING JEWELLERY ROBBERY.
div.p: DARING JEWELLERY ROBBERY.
£4OO WORTH TAKEN.

It is reported that on Thursday night a man went to Mr. Bennett's, jeweller's, Lime-st., Preston, and asked to look at a clock hanging at the door. When Mr. Bennett returned to the shop he missed from the window a case containing sixty rings valued at about £4OO. It is supposed that a confederate of the first man entered the shop while Mr. Bennett was at the door. Efforts to trace the thieves are as yet unsuccessful.

div.head: • -4,-- SCANDALOUS IF TRUE.
div.p: • -4,-- SCANDALOUS IF TRUE.

In connection with Thursday's meeting in the Jerusa- lem Chamber "to raise a fund to meet the claims upon the estate by the late Archbishop Magee," it is stated that in one way or another his translation to York cost the late Archbishop no less a sum than £7,000. In other words, to obtain a promotion the increased income at- taching to which he did not live to enjoy, Dr. Magee wag mulcted in a sum equivalent to eighteen months' income of the see he resigned. The "Times," which is respon- sible for this statement, says it cannot profess to explain it.

div.head: PENSIONS IN OLD AGE.
div.p: PENSIONS IN OLD AGE.

Mr. Chamberlain has written to the editor of the "Rural World" in explanation of his old age pension scheme. He describes as shocking a condition of things under which one in two of the industrial population who may reach the age of 65 is doomed to end his life in receipt of pauper relief. Hitherto neither the post office nor the great friendly societies have succeeded in induc- ing the working classes to make any provision against old age. As to compuision, Mr. Chamberlain admits that there are great difficulties in the way. After consultation with an actuary he has come to the conclusion that it would be impossible to make any scheme for annuities at the age of sixty without requiring a larger contribution than workmen are able or willing to pay.

MURDER AND MUTILATION OF A CHILD.

The body of a child, shockingly mutilated, was found in the archway of the Leeds Municipal Buildings at midnight on Wednesday. Inquiry resulted in the identification of the body as that of Barbara Waterhouse, aged five years,who disappeared from her home at Hors- forth last Saturday. The child had evidently been murdered. The only clue to the identity of the murderer possessed by the notice is an old plaid shawl in which the body was wrapped. No arrests have been made.

div.head: INQUEST.
div.p: THE INQUEST.

The inquest was held yesterday afternoon at the Town Hall, before the borough coroner. After the evidence of the parents of the child, who was five years old, had been given, Dr. Ward, police surgeon, de.icribed the re. suit of the post-mortem examination he had made in conjunction with Dr. Smith. There were about sfty wounds of different kinds on the body, some of them cuts, several stabs, and most of them of a terrible character. The most serious extended from the pit of the stomach to the chest, and this in Dr. Ward's opinion, was the one that caused death, as it was the only wound which had bled. The lower part of the body was shockingly mutilated, and the legs carved and hacked to such an extent as to be almost severed from the body. There were also cuts on the fingers which indicated that the deceased had deter- minedly resisted the assassin. he had evi4ently been murdered from twenty-four to forty hours before the body was found. The inquiry was adjourned, as the Coroner remarked at the opening that it was not an ordinary case of murder, and would require the most searching investigation on the part of the police.

div.head: WIEDMANN-WALPOLE CASE:
div.p: THE WIEDMANN-WALPOLE CASE:

The Wiedemann-Walpole breach of promise case came before Baron Pollock and a special jury in the Queen's Bench Divsion on Wednesday. The action had been twice previously before the Court. On the first occasion plaintiff was non-suited, and on the second hearing the jury decided in favour of the Hon. Robert Horace Wal- pole, the defendant. Plaintiff sought to recover £20,000 damages for breach of promise of marriage and libel. Counsel for the plaintiff had not concluded his opening statement when the court adjourned. The breach of promise action, Wiedmann v. Walpole, was resumed on Thursday in the Queen's Bench, before Barron Pollock. Miss Wiedmann went into the box and repeated the statement made by her at the previous trials,that defendant came into her bedroom at Constant- inople and promised her marriage and seduced her against her will. He afterwards gave her a signet ring. Mr. Lockwood, for defendant, said the ring belonged to Mr. Walpole. The question was, how plaintiff obtained ir. Plaintiff, continuing, spoke of her stormy interview with defendant's mother.

Yesterday the suit was resumed before Baron Pollock. The plaintiff, in .cross-examination, said she knew a man named Crenneville. Mr. Lockwood put in a copy of a statement made by one Victor Crenneville at Pera, in which he said he had had passing relations in 1881 with a person named Valerie .Wiedemann, through payment of money, and who had tried to strangle him, whereupon he asked the protection of the Consul.—Cross-examined by Mr. Lockwood, the plaintiff swore she was not the Valerie Wiedemann mentioned, and that she never told the defendant an officer took her to Constantinople. When defendant entered her room she did not scream. Plaintiff subsequently said she screamed, and fought for her virtue.

The extensive timber yard of Messrs. Gorse and Tap- ping, situate near Dalston Junction, was destroyed by fire on Thursday morning. A " Times " Lisbon telegram states that the King pre- sided on Thursday morning at a council to sanction the law relating to the treaty to be signed by Sir G. Petro and Sennor Val bora.
