div.head: PRESTON BROOK.
div.p: PRESTON BROOK.

MissioN Roost.—The Church services on Sunday was conducted by the Rev. Morley Stevenson, of Warrington, Training College, owing to the absence ;of the Vicar, the Rev. Thomas Nit ScaoLAns TREAT. —On Monday afternoon about 40 of the Sunday scholars of the Wesleyan Chapel were enter- tained to tea in the sthoolroom. After tea they assembled in a field lent by Mr. Frodsham;of Aston. Here sports consisting of football, crisket, racing, and other amuse- ments, for which prizes were given, were freely indulged in until nine o'clock, when they were dispersed to their homes, all having spent an enjoyable evening. WESLEYAN CHAPEL—The Sunday school anniversary sermons in connection with the Ashton-lane Chapel were preached on Sunday. Both serviees were well attended, especially that in the evening, and the preacher on both occasions was the Rev. J. Judson, of Halton. Suitable sacred pieces and hymns were creditably rendered by the scholars and choir, assisted by a few friends. The collections were in excess of last year, amounting to over £9.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

IMPROVEMENT AT FRODSRAM BRIDGE.—A new exten- sion to the already extensive flour mills of Messrs. Thomas Rigby and Sons, of Frodshain Bridge, is in course of erection, Mr. Davies, of Frodshans, being the contractor. This may be reared as an indication of the desire of the firm to be ready to avail of the increased facility for trade which will be offered by the new Canal, which is but a short distance away, and is accessible from the Weaver, which passes close to the mill. ANNIVERSARY SERMONS.—The annual sermons on behalf of the Wesleyan Sunday School were preached in the Trinity Chapel on Sunday, morning and evening, by the Rev. R. Waddy Moss, of Didsbtiry College. In the afternoon a special service was conducted by Mr. Moss, which was in part a flower service, the children and friends having been requested to bring flowers, which were subsequently to be distributed to the sick people in the district, and the remainder to be sent to the Man- chester Flower Mission. The services were well at- tended, particularly the evening one. The choir and scholars accompanied on the organ and some seven stringedinstruments, . rendered the special hymns and anthem, " Awake ! put on strength," in a fairly credit- able manner. The collections realised £lB. The chapel and premises presented a very nice appearance, having been painted and decorated, the arch over the orchestra and the vestibule being very much admired.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.
THE INFLUENZA.

The epidemic is not yet at an end at Penketh, and it is reported in the village on Tuesday evening, that no fewer than seven persons in one house were suffering from the disease. WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY. On Sunday, the annual anniversary services in connection with the Wesleyan Sunday School, took place. Preacher, the Rev. A. H. Walker, 8.A., of Didsbury College. There were good congregations at all the services, except the morning. A power- ful discourse was preached in the morning from the text contained in St. John iv. 39-42; in the evening the text was selected from St. Luke xv., the parable of the Prodigal Son. In the evening two anthems were sung by the choir, entitled "The Lord is my Shepherd," by Macfarren, and "The radiant morn has passed away," by Woodward. These were much appreciated. In the afternoon the sacred cantata, "The Good Shepherd," by Pattison, was rendered by , the choir, conducted by Mr. J. Watson, organist Mr, W. J. Wigfleld. The singing during the day was everything that could be desired, and reflected the greatest credit on the conductor and organist. The treble parts in the duets, solos, quartets, &c., were sung by Misses noutledge, Hobson, Mainley, Allan Watson. and Hut-zhes, Boardman, and H. Mainley, and the contralto parts by Allan Watson, C. Cooke, J. Watson, and E. Ashton. The tenors were Messrs. J. T. Budden, A. Seed, P. Hughes, and W. T. Wilkinson. and Mr. James Smith, bass. Col- lections were taken at each service in aid of the school funds, amounting in all to .£22 Bs., being a decrease of several pounds on last year.

The extensive timber yard at Dalston Junction, occu- pied by Messrs. Corse and Tapping, was on Thursday en- tirely destroyed by tire. Serious rioting is report•d at Bremerhaven in connec- tion with the strike of stokers and coal trimmers, the dis- turbance reaching such a pitch that he police were com- pelled to charge with drawn swords. THE PORTUGESE IN AFRICA. REVOLT OF NATIVES.

A Reuter's telegram from Mozambique reports the re- volt of 3,000 or 4,000 natives against Portuguese rule on the Pungwe River, and that they had declared for the British. Portugese troops are being hurried up.

div.head: DEATHS FROM INFLUENZA.
div.p: DEATHS FROM INFLUENZA.

From inquiry midi) from the Medical Officer of Health 'for Warrington we learn that there was a further increase last week in the fatality from influ- ,euza in Varrington. The deaths directly referable to this disease have, with some little intermission, ,gradually risen during the six weeks ended June 6th as follows :—Week ended May 2nd, 3; week ended May 9th, 1; week ended May 23rd, 4 ; week ended May 30th, 7; week ended, June 6th, 13. During the same period the death-rate from zymo- tic disease has been very low, 11 per 1000, and the deaths from lung disease have been 51 as against 23 in the corresponding weeks of 1890. DEATH OF A CHESHIRE CLERGYMAN. The death took place at Loyalty-place, Stockport, on Thursday morning, suddenly, from an attack of in- fluenza, of the Rev. Matthew Pugh, M.A., a well-known Cheshire clergyman, in his seventy-third year. The deceased gentleman was formerly headmaster of Congle- ton and Rishworth Grammar Schools, then vicar of Marple, and latterly, up to a few years ago, the rector of :St. Thomas's; StoclFport.
LOCAL CASES AT COUNTY SESSIONS.

The Liverpool County Intermediate Sessions were held on Tuesday and Wednesday; Mr. Hugh Per- kins, the chairman, presiding in the first, and Sir William B. Forwood, the deputy-chairman, in the second, court. The following were the local cases:—
Richard Tankiea, 25, labourer, was committed to jail for twelve months on a charge of having, at Widnes, unlawfully assaulted a girl named Cathetine M•Nichol- -son.
Thomas Costello, 28, labourer, was sentenced to three months' imprisonment for having, at Widnes, on the 26th ult, wounded 'William M‘Donald.

SENTENCES.—WiIIiam Kennedy (36),labourer,was com- mitted for six months with hard labour for assaulting,at Ashton-in-Makerfield, on the Bth ult., Alice Littler. William Stewart (36)., labourer, was sent to gaol for eighteen months with hard labour,for having,at, Widnes, assaulted a girl named Ellen Mulligan. ACQUITTED.—Robert Morris, a labourer, was acquitted one charge of having attempted to commit a criminal- assault on a boy at Widnes, on the 7th inst. POLISH LIFE AT WieNEs.—Frank' Miller, and Martin' Miller surrendered to bail on a charge of having at Widnes, on the 25th April, wounded Dominic Davitsk.— Mr. Cooper and Mr. Formby prosecuted,and Mr. Segar ap- peared for the defence. For the prosecution it was stated that the prisoners attacked Davitsk on the 25th April, and seriously wounded him about the head. Witnesses were, however, called for the defence to prove that on the night in question no assault ha'd been committed by the prisoners on Davitsk, as they were in company with two other men all the even- ing. The parties in the case were Poles, and it was elisited during the hearing that there were a number of Poles in Widnes, employed at the chemical works. A police-constable said that the Poles bore a very bad char- acter in the borough some years ago, but that they were not so bad now. Many of the Poles were in the habit of drinking, gambling, and fighting, and breaking each other's heads on Saturday nights.—Mr. Cooper : The Poles are given to gambling ?—The Officer: Yes.—Mr. Cooper: Do they play baccarat ? (Laughter.)—The Officer : I don't know. I don't understand the game.— Mr. Segar Are the prisoners inert of good character ? The Officer: Yes I know them very well.—The prisoners were found not guilty, and were discharged.—This con- cluded the business of the sessions.
INQUESTS AT RUNCORN.
Mr. J. E. Worsley, coroner for the honour and fee of llalton, on Moday held an inquest at the Run- corn Police Court, on the body of Margaret Nuttall, who was

DILOWNED IN THE BOTTOM LOCKS on the Friday night previous. The girl, who was nearly five years of age, lived with her parents on board the flat John, belonging to Mr. S. Taylor, and on Friday evening she was playing on the deck. After a lapse of some time the mother came on the deck, but could see nothing of her daughter, and she raised an alarm. James Molyneaux a canal constable, dragged the lock, and found the dead body of the child. A verdict of "Acci- dental death" was returned.

div.head: WESTON POINT DEATH TRAP.
div.p: WESTON POINT DEATH TRAP.

At the Weaver Hotel, Weston Point, on Monday, Mr. Worsley held an inquest on the body of Walter Head, 20 years of age, who was cook on board the schooner "Old Henry." The evidence showed that on Wednes- day evening the deceased was in Runcorn and met with some friends from St. Valerie. He had some drink, but was quite capable of taking care of himself, when a sea- man named Wm. Foster left him in Percival-lane, shortly after ten o'clock. He had not turned up at the schooner on the following morning, and on Saturday morning his dead body was found by P.C. Hamersley near the iron bridge in the Weeton caned. Ilia watch had stopped at ten minutes past twelve. It was a very wet and dark night when the deceased was missing. The Coroner commented on the dangerous road the deceased had to traverse to get to his ship, but said it was of no use talking as nothing was done to remedy it.—A jury- man suggested that if an influential deputation waited upon Major Orred that gentleman, who had shown a generous disposition in the past, would be willing to open out a new road to Weston Point.—The Coroner said it was unfortunate that no one could be made res- ponsible for the numerous deaths caused by the present means of communication.—A verdict of " Found drowned" was recorded.

div.head: KILLED ON TRH SKIP CANAL.
div.p: KILLED ON TRH SKIP CANAL.

At the Half Way House, Flalton•road, an Monday, Mr. J. E. Worsley, the coroner, held an inquest on the body of Herbert Francis, stepson of P.C. Boyle. On the 24th April, Francis, who is 17 years of age, was crushed. between the buffers of the locomotive of a wagon on the ; Ship Canal railway at the Big Field, and he was severely injured. He was taken to the Latchford Hospital, where a few weeks ago he was discharged as convaleseent,:and returned home. Subsequently he became unwell and died on Friday. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.

div.head: FAMILY DISPUTE.
div.p: A FAMILY DISPUTE.

At the Warrington County Court, on Thursday. Judge Ffoulkes had trfore him the case of Hill v. Horrocks. The case had been part heard on the 28th ult., when his Honour suggested that as the dispute was a family matter some amicable settlement might be made, and the case was adjourned accordingly. The plaintiff, John Hill, hinge maker, Ashton, sued Henry Horrocks, Winwick, for the return of a number of articles of furniture or their value, £5O. Mr. Forshaw, (Messrs. P. Davies and Forshaw), appeared for the plain- tiff and Mr. IL Dobson junr., (instructed by Mr. Arthur Browne) for the defendant. Mr. Forshaw informed his Honour that he had endeavoured to bring the matter to a settlement but had failed to do so. It appears that the plaintiff married the defendant's daughter in 1877, and they went to reside at Go'borne. In 1884, however, the plaintiff and his wife went to reside with the defen- dant at his request at Winwick and took with them the furniture in question. The plailitiff worked at the paper mill at Newton until December, 1890, when he went to work at Leigh. He had to take lodgings there, but went over to Winwick every fortnight to see his wife and child- ren, and paid her 155., 18s., and £1 per week up to the 18th of April. Since the 21st of February the defendant had refused the complainant admission into his house and had locked the door against him. The plaintiff de- manded his furniture but the defendant refused to give it up. On the 2nd of May the plaintiff wrote to his wife telling her that he had taken a house at Golborne, and asked her to come and live with him, but she had taken no notice of his letter. With respect to the counter- claim the plaintiff said he had borrowed no money from the defendant and that he had regularly allowed his wife wages, except when he was out of work, for about a month. Mr. Dobson for the defence contended that most of the furniture claimed belonged to the plaintiff's wife, and that the defendant had left his wife and the defendant had been obliged to keep her. She, however, admitted that she had sold a piano for £8 and also two chairs, which belonged to the plaintiff, for maintenance. His Honour gave judgment for the 13laintiff both on the claim and eounter-claim,the goads to be returned within a week or their value,£3o, and ls.damages for detention, with costs on claim and counter-claim.

Mr. Beal, the father of the London Municipal Reform Movement, died on Thursday. Several persona have been killed and many injured by a hurricane in the district of Brody. East Galicia. Sir Wilfrid Lawson, M. P., was on Thursday entertained at breakfast by the Liverpool and District Direct Veto League. -
A-New York telezram says the corps are so advanced that what is expected to prove a brilliant harvest has already begun.

French outrages on foreigners continue to be reported front China. An English missinnary and a Customs officer have been murdered near Kinkiang. The railway passengers recently captured by brigands in Turkey were released on Monday on payment of £B,OOO as ransom. Troops will now start in pur- suit.
The Marquis of Hartington has signified his acceptance of the chairmanship of the Blakowell Board of Guar- dians, in succession to the late Lord Edward Caven- dish.
From a letter received in Liverpool on Monday it appears that Mr. de Cobain, M.P., is residing at Bilbao, in apartments with an English family who keep a school for children.
The stipendiary magistrate at Cardiff. who caused Mr. Wilaon, of the Seamen's Union, to be ejected from his court the other day, has intimated his readiness to hear Mr. Wilson's application.
LATEST NEWS.

CRICKET. • Notts innings closed yesterday for 336. COLLISION AT SEA. The mail boat Duchess of Albany ran into and sank the ketch Mary Offey, of Harwich, in the Solent yester- day morning. The crew of the latter were saved. COLLISION BETWEEN GOODS TRAINS. Two goods trains collided yesterday at Moreton, near Hereford. Several wagons went off the line, and the guard was slightly injured. The mail trains were also delayed. FALL OF THE ROOF OF A CHAPEL. ONE MAN KILLED.

The roof a Wesleyan chapel f-ell in at Winsford, Che- shire, yesterday afternoon, killing one man outright.and seriously injuring five more, some of whom are not ex- pected to recover. DEATH OF A BARONET. A Hereford corzespondent telegraphs :—Sir Harford James Jones Brydges, Bart., died on Thursday night, at his residence, Boultibrook, Presteign. Deceased, who was the second baronet, was born May 30th, 1808. The title is now extinct. •

SCOTTISH SHOOTING CHAMPIONSHIP. At Darnley Range, near Glasgow, yesterday afternoon, Corporal Ritchie, secretary of the Renfrewshire Volun- APers, won the Scottish Shooting Championship Cup, and £lOO, with a score of 106 points. There were 60 com- petitors, including many English volunteers. FUNERAL SERVICE IN WESTMINSTER ABBEY. Yesterday a special service was held in Westminster Abbey,in memory of the late Sir John Macdonald, Premier of Canada. There was a good attendance, and amongst those present were Lord Knutsforcl, Lord Cranbrook,and Mr. W. H. Smith. Representatives were also present of the Queen and other members of the Royal Family.
SIR WILLIAM GORDON-CUMMING REMOVED
FROM THE ARMY.

It is notified in last night's " Gazette " that Major and Lieut.-Colonel Sir William Gordon-Cumming has been removed from the Army, "Her Majesty having no fur- ther occasion for his services." The removal is dated the 10th inst.

COUNTY COUNCIL ELECTIONS. Copies of the billibrought in on Th ursday night by Mr. Ritchie, in reference to County Council elections, were issued yesterday. The bill fiXB4 the ordinary day of the election for March 8, and the election of chairman and aldermen for March 16. The county register is to be completed before the 20th day of December in every year. coming into operation on the first day of the next January. The bill further provided that the chairman, aldermen, and councillors, whose term of office would but for this bill expire on the ordinary day of election in November next after the passing of the bill shall go out of office on the next day of election fixed by the bill.
MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL
IMPORTANT DECISION.

The Hybrid Committee of the House of Commons which on Thursday passed the preamble of the Man- chester Ship Canal (Loan) Bill, met yesterday morning to proceed with the consideration of the clauses. Con- siderable discussion followed on the financial features-of the bill, and in reference to the proposal that the sink- ing fund should not commence for ten years, which was opposed by the Local Government Board, the Corpora- tion agreed to aceept five years. This was adopted by the Conunittee. In reply to Sir R. Temple, Mr. Moulton, Q.C.,who appeared for the Corporation, stated that there was no precedent,he believed,for a loan of this description. Upon the consideration of the proviso in clause 28, under which the Corporation asked for power to hand over to the Canal Company any profit which the Cor- poration might make through lending the £3,000,000, a long discussion took place. The Chairman announced the decision of the Committee to strike out the proviso. The effect of this decision is that any profit accruing from the loan will go to the benefit of the ratepayer. Eventually all the clauses were disposed of, the Com- mittee deciding that the proposal that there should be five directors from the Corporation on the Board of the Company should be retained. The proceedings then closed, the Bill being ordered to be "reported to the House.

div.head: YESTERDAY'S PAUL lAMEN T. HOUSE OF LORDS.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S PAUL lAMEN T. HOUSE OF LORDS.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a qua) ter past four: The North Sea Fisheries Bill was read a first time. CnorrEn CoLoursenou.—The Duke of ARGYLL called attention to the report of the Colonisation Committee of the House of Commons. He referred to the fact that, al- though the scope of inquiry referred to the congested dis- tricts in the United Kingdom, it was practically limited to the Hebrides and the West of Scotland. The Marquis of LOTHIAN believed if the crofters could be induced to emigrate, they would, by their own industry, become self-supporting. Her Majesty's Government was in com- munication with the Government of British Columbia, and he thought it probable that the terms suggested would be accepted. The House adjourned at six o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.

The Speaker took the chair shortly after thre* o'clock. THH MANCHESTER SiP CANAL BILL.—ThP report of the Select Committee on the Manchester Ship Canal Bill was brought up by Sir Henry Selwin-Ibbetson and ordered to lie on the table.
EVICTIONS IN IRELAND.-Mr. Parnell brought in a bill to facilitate the reinstatement of evicted tenants in Ire- land.

THE L AND PURCHASE BlLL—Consideration was re- sumed on the report of the Irish Land Purchase Bill.— Mr. KEAY moved a verbal amendment underwhich he pro- posed to discuss the general financial proposals of the bill. —The CHIEF SECRETARY objected, and the SPEAKER called Mr. Keay to order.—The amendment was negatived.— Mr. SEXTON moved an amendment providing that no guaranteed land stock should be issued by way of ad- vance for the purchase of any holding until after the es- tablishment of County Councils.—Mr. BALFOUR opposed the amendment.—The House divided upon the amend- ment, which was defeated by 175 to 106.

div.head: LONDON BUSMEN'S STRIKE.
div.p: LONDON BUSMEN'S STRIKE.

The Omnibus Strike continued in London on Thursday without any signs on either side of yielding. Mr. Sutherst wrote to the omnibus Com- panies on Thursday morning, saying he understands the companies will meet the men's wishes regarding the twelve hours day, and asking for a conference with the Joint Board to discuss the matter definitely. The Joint directors met on Thursday morning, and in reply to Mr. Sutherst's letter, directed their secretary to inform Mr. Sutherst that a conference was unnecessary, and that the working day referred to in the directors' manifesto was intended to be one of twelve consecutive hours as nearly as possible. It is understood they have decided that the men must resume work on the terms already offered, and that otherwise new hands will be engaged. The Press Association says yesterday was the sixth day of the London 'bus strike, and the vehicles of the General Omnibus Company and Road Car Company were again absent from the streets, their yards being closely picketed as usual, and guarded by policemen. Funds for the strikers are coming in,and special entertainments are being organised on the men's behalf: The 'bus men will take part in the demonstrations of the laundresses and the railway workers in Hyde Park on Sunday. The Lord Mayor has discussed the situation with the strike leaders and the company's directors. A conciliatory spirit was manifested on both sides. LATEST.—.A SETTLEMENT EFFECTED.

A telegram to hand says :—" A settlement of the ominous strike, arranged through the mediation of the Lord Mayor of London, has been been accepted by tha companies and the men, and will be announced at the mass meeting to-night."
At the Forest of Dean on Thursday night Sir Charles Nike finally accepted the invitation to contest the con- stituency at the next election.

A Ctiester correspondent telegraphs that Mr. W. Willis, Q.C., is mentionod as a probable candidate to contest Chester against Mr. Yerburgh, M.P. Seven thousand men in the shipbuilding yards in the upper reaches of the Clyde struck work on Monday against the proposed reduction of 5. per cent. in their wages.

MUNICIPAL ELECTION. TO THE ELECTORS OF WHITECROSS WARD. LADIEs AND GENTLEMEN,—A vacancy has been caused in your Ward through the elevation of Councillor Greenall to the Aldermanic Bench, and, as I have been requested `by a large number of ratepayers to become a candidate for the vacant post, I beg to offer myself for your suffrages. I think I may claim to be well-known to most of you as a resident in the Ward. I am glad to see that the Baths are to be enlarged and improved. I am of opinion that steps should be taken to effect a reduction in the price of Gas ; and I am in favour of a Stipendiary Magistrate, if an appointment can be made without being a burden on the rates. I am strongly of opinion that there should be a Public Inquiry as to the Intercepting Depots and Longfnrd Works. In my judgment, the ratepayers are at all times entitled to have their grievances inquir-d into, and to know how their money is being spent. At the same time, I am desirous of assisting the Sanitary Committee in dealing with insanitary dwellings, and doing what they can to make the homes of working-men healthier and more comfortable. Trusting to obtain your support on the day of election, I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient Servant, GEO. PLUMPTON. 125, Lovely-lane, Warrington, June sth, 1891. MUNICIPAL ELECTION. WHITECROSS WARD. TO THE BURGESSES OF THE WAD. LADIES ANDGENTLENIEN, —At the invitation of a large and influential body of ratepayers. I have much pleasure in again ,offering myself for election as your representative, on Mon- day, June 15th. I have, as many of you know, for over ten years taken an active part and interest in all matters calcu- lated to benefit the ratepayers generally, and to improve our town. Being a resident in your Ward, as well as a native of War- rington, my interests and yours are the same ; you may therefore depend upon my giving my best attention to all matters promoted to improve the streets, and working-men's dwellings in the Ward. lam strongly in favour of all Cor- poration contracts being given to Warrington men, and that no tender be accepted where sweating is carried on. I am most favourably disposed towards large and commo- dousbatbs being erected at once, and opened free on certain days to all school -children under control of their teachers ; and also that the prices charged. especially for the swimming baths, shall be as low as possible, so as to encourage the art of swimming amongst all, which is now impossible, owing to the prohibitive charge. I pledge myself, if returneil, to make it my aim, at all times, to bring forward and support measures calculated to secure the greatest com- fort and convenience, of the Burgesses. I am, yours faithfully, MirliED WOODS. 93, Bewsey-road, Warrington, June sth, 1891.

NOTICE IS HEREBY GlVEN,that the next GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for the County of Chester will be holden at the CASTLE OF CHESTER, in and for the said County, on MONDAY, the 29th day of June instant, at Half-past Eleven o'ulock:in the Forenoon when the Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing (fall Appeals arising within the Hundreds of Broxton, Eddisbury, Nantwich and Wirral', forming the Chester District; and the trials of all prisoners com- mitted from such Hundreds, will take place at such Ses- sions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Chester Dis- trict must be in attendance at the Castle of Chester, at the opening of Court on MONDAY, the 29th day of June instant, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. THE COURT will he Adjourned to the Court House, Nether, Knutsford, on WEDNESDAY, the Ist day of July next, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, when another Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hundreds of Bucklow, Mac- clesfield,and Northwich, forming the Knutsford District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from the last- mentioned Hundreds will take place at such Adjourned Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Knutsford District must be in attendance at the Court House,Knuts- ford, at the opening of the Court on WEDNESDAY, the Ist day of July next, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk of the Peace for the County of Chester. Chester, Bth June,lB9l.

MOURNING ANNO UNCEMENT. "THE LAST ENEMY IS DEATH ! " The custom of wearing black for the dead dates back to the times of the Remans, since when it has always been popul.tr amongst Western nations, The 'great mortality of this country, considering its sanitary arrangements, has given birth to a number of shops exclusively for the SALE OF MOURNING.
